Abnormal Uterine Bleeding

abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) from menarche to after menopause · adolescent anovulation and bleeding disorders, fibroids, bleeding after menopause · treat the consequence, not the findingIs she pregnant, is there a consequence, and is she still in the physiologic state that the benign explanation needs?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Classify by PALM-COEIN (structural: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy and hyperplasia; nonstructural: coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial, iatrogenic, not otherwise classified). Every patient is tested for pregnancy and anemia first. For heavy menses the levonorgestrel intrauterine device (IUD) is the most effective medical therapy.

Reassurance requires two things: a benign cause and an acceptable consequence. Anemia is a consequence, and normal physiology does not make it acceptable.

  • Adolescent anovulation: normal in the first 1 to 2 years after menarche, from an immature hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis; irregular, heavy and painless, and a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Bleeding-disorder screen: heavy bleeding since the very first period, a family history of abnormal bleeding, frequent bruising, bleeding gums, epistaxis, postpartum hemorrhage, or bleeding with surgical and dental procedures. Bleeding disorders are found in about 20% of adolescents evaluated for heavy menses (33% of those hospitalized): most commonly von Willebrand disease, platelet function defects, thrombocytopenia and clotting factor deficiencies.
  • Fibroids (leiomyomas): symptoms, not size, drive treatment. Impressive anatomy (markedly enlarged, multiple, intramural, pedunculated) does not demand action when every symptom domain is negative; asymptomatic fibroids get observation.
  • Postmenopausal bleeding: no period for over a year means she is postmenopausal, and any bleeding after 12 months of amenorrhea is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Amount and duration are irrelevant; a single episode of spotting counts.
  • Endometrial sampling: at 45 or older with abnormal bleeding; younger with a significant history of unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or failed medical management; after menopause by the workup below.

Mechanism: the immature axis makes no luteinizing hormone (LH) surge, so anovulation follows; without a corpus luteum there is no progesterone. Unopposed estrogen drives continuous proliferation with no secretory differentiation, and the lining outgrows its blood supply and sheds unpredictably. Progesterone converts proliferative to secretory endometrium and produces organized withdrawal bleeding.

Defining criteria Normal adolescent cycle – every 21 to 45 days (adults 24 to 38), lasting 7 days or fewer, 3 to 6 products a day or fewer · Painless heavy irregular bleeding – the anovulatory signature; ovulatory cycles are crampy · Reassurance requires – a benign cause and an acceptable consequence; anemia is not an acceptable consequence
Diagnosis
Adolescent bleeding: clue, diagnosis, confirmation
ClueDiagnosisConfirms, then
Irregular, heavy, painless, within 2 years of menarcheAnovulation from an immature axisClinical, after a negative pregnancy test, complete blood count and ferritin; treat if anemic, otherwise reassure
Heavy since the very first period, bruising, epistaxis, family historyVon Willebrand diseaseLow von Willebrand factor activity; often repeated because levels vary; then hematology
Hirsutism, acne, obesity, acanthosis nigricansPolycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)Androgens and glucose; in adolescents both hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction, no ultrasound; then a combined oral contraceptive
GalactorrheaProlactinomaHigh prolactin with pregnancy and hypothyroidism excluded; pituitary magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows the adenoma; then cabergoline
Weight loss, athlete, low body mass indexFunctional hypothalamic amenorrhea (female athlete triad)Low LH, follicle-stimulating hormone and estradiol once pregnancy, thyroid and prolactin causes are excluded; restore energy balance, check bone density
Any sexually active patientPregnancyPregnancy test before anything else; quantitative human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and ultrasound to locate it
Fibroid location determines the symptom Submucosal: heavy bleeding and infertility or pregnancy loss, the most symptomatic despite often being the smallest. Intramural: bleeding and bulk. Subserosal or pedunculated: pressure, and can torse. Cervical: obstruction. Fibroids are estrogen- and progesterone-dependent and regress after menopause, so they cannot explain postmenopausal bleeding.
The enlarged uterus: the differential
DiagnosisUterusThe tell
LeiomyomaIrregular, firm, lumpy, mobileHeavy menses; regresses after menopause
AdenomyosisGlobular, symmetric, boggy, tenderSevere dysmenorrhea; MRI shows a thickened junctional zone
PregnancySymmetric, softAmenorrhea, then beta-hCG
Endometrial cancerNormal or enlargedPostmenopausal bleeding, then biopsy
LeiomyosarcomaRapidly enlarging, especially after menopauseDoes not arise from a leiomyoma; avoid morcellation
Treat a fibroid only for a consequence Heavy or prolonged menses, especially with anemia. Bulk symptoms: pressure, urinary frequency, constipation, hydronephrosis. Pelvic pain or dyspareunia. Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss (submucosal). Rapid growth, or any growth after menopause: leiomyosarcoma concern.
After menopause About 90% of endometrial cancer presents with postmenopausal bleeding, and about 9 to 10% of postmenopausal bleeding is cancer. Atrophy is the most common cause, about 60%, but a diagnosis of exclusion: a pale vagina with minimal rugation does not justify reassurance.
Practice
  1. 17-year-old girl has 3 weeks of irregular vaginal bleeding Sexually active with one partner; uses condoms inconsistently Last normal period 7 weeks ago No pelvic pain BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min · Afebrile → Pregnancy test first → in any sexually active patient the pregnancy test comes before anything else; every patient with abnormal bleeding is tested for pregnancy and anemia. A positive test leads to a quantitative hCG level and ultrasound to locate the pregnancy. A complete blood count and ferritin follow the pregnancy test; they do not replace it
  2. 14-year-old girl has irregular, heavy, painless periods since menarche 18 months ago Not bothered by the bleeding No bruising, nosebleeds or family bleeding history Afebrile · HR 78/min · hemoglobin 13 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative → Reassurance + menstrual calendar → painless irregular bleeding within 2 years of menarche is anovulation from an immature axis, normal for her age. The pregnancy test is negative, nothing suggests a bleeding disorder, and she is not anemic, so there is no consequence to treat: reassure and keep a menstrual calendar. A combined oral contraceptive treats a consequence she does not have. Endometrial biopsy under 45 needs a significant history of unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or failed medical management, and her pattern is the expected one 18 months after menarche
  3. 15-year-old girl has had heavy periods since her first period 2 years ago Bruises easily; frequent nosebleeds Her mother bled heavily after a dental extraction HR 92/min · hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · platelets 260,000/mm³ · urine pregnancy test negative → Von Willebrand factor antigen, activity and factor VIII → heavy bleeding since menarche with bruising, nosebleeds and a family history is the bleeding-disorder screen; bleeding disorders are found in about 20% of adolescents evaluated for heavy menses. Order von Willebrand factor antigen, activity (ristocetin cofactor) and factor VIII, often repeated because levels vary over time, and work with hematology. The prothrombin time is normal in most patients with von Willebrand disease and the partial thromboplastin time is normal in mild disease, so alone they do not exclude it; a platelet count screens for thrombocytopenia, a different disorder
  4. 16-year-old girl has 10 days of heavy vaginal bleeding, soaking a pad every hour Light-headed on standing Urine pregnancy test negative BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · hemoglobin 6.8 g/dL · Afebrile → Admit for intravenous conjugated estrogen → a hemodynamically unstable adolescent, or one actively bleeding heavily, is hospitalized. Without contraindications to estrogen, give intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 to 6 hours (25 mg, for 24 hours), then taper with a high-dose combined pill; tranexamic acid may be added to stop bleeding, and transfuse for instability. Outpatient pills are for the stable patient, and tranexamic acid alone leaves out the admission and the hormone
  5. 16-year-old girl has heavy but regular periods lasting 8 days Wants treatment but declines any hormonal medication Bleeding-disorder testing normal; not sexually active hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL · ferritin 14 ng/mL · urine pregnancy test negative → Tranexamic acid → oral tranexamic acid is an effective, well-tolerated nonhormonal choice, reducing blood loss by 26 to 54%; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the other. Both distractors are hormonal, which she declines. Give iron for the anemia
  6. 16-year-old girl has had irregular periods since menarche 4 years ago Facial hair and acne for 2 years dark velvety skin on the back of the neck body mass index 34 kg/m² · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Polycystic ovary syndrome → hirsutism and acne (hyperandrogenism) with ovulatory dysfunction, obesity and acanthosis nigricans: in adolescents both features are required and ultrasound is not used. Check androgens and glucose, then a combined oral contraceptive. Atypical (nonclassic) congenital adrenal hyperplasia can mimic it and is excluded with a serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone, which may need an adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test. Virilization, rapid progression, or androgen levels well above the reference range point to an ovarian or adrenal neoplasm
  7. 17-year-old girl has had no period for 5 months Milky discharge from both nipples Not sexually active; no medications BP 112/70 mm Hg · body mass index 21 kg/m² · urine pregnancy test negative → Prolactin → galactorrhea with amenorrhea: measure prolactin. A high level, with pregnancy and hypothyroidism excluded, leads to pituitary MRI to show the adenoma; cabergoline treats it. Thyroid-stimulating hormone alone misses the prolactin, and a pelvic ultrasound looks at the wrong organ
  8. 17-year-old girl who runs cross-country has had no period for 6 months Lost 7 kg this season Menarche at 13; regular periods until this year body mass index 17 kg/m² · HR 48/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea → weight loss in an athlete with a low body mass index: the female athlete triad. Luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and estradiol are low once pregnancy, thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin are excluded; restore energy balance and check bone density. Polycystic ovary syndrome brings hirsutism and acne, often with overweight or obesity, and primary ovarian insufficiency a high follicle-stimulating hormone
  9. 17-year-old girl has 2 years of irregular heavy bleeding despite 6 months of a combined oral contraceptive Infrequent periods for years before starting the pill body mass index 41 kg/m² · hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative → Endometrial biopsy → obesity and prolonged anovulation are years of unopposed estrogen, and medical management has failed: endometrial sampling is indicated in a younger patient with a significant history of unopposed estrogen exposure, persistent bleeding or ineffective medical management. An ultrasound can be considered after failed initial management, but alone it does not sample the endometrium; continuing a failed pill delays the diagnosis
  10. 38-year-old woman has 1 year of heavy periods lasting 9 days Wants more children in a few years ultrasound shows two intramural fibroids, cavity normal hemoglobin 9 g/dL · BP 118/74 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative → Levonorgestrel IUD → heavy bleeding with anemia is a consequence worth treating. The levonorgestrel intrauterine device is more effective than other medical therapies for heavy menstrual bleeding (71 to 95% less blood loss): first-line medical therapy, with iron. Hysterectomy ends the fertility she wants, and a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist is a short-term bridge to surgery
  11. 47-year-old woman has 4 months of heavy, irregular periods Previously regular cycles; no medications uterus normal size on bimanual exam BP 128/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative → Endometrial biopsy regardless of ultrasound findings → at 45 or older, abnormal bleeding gets endometrial sampling, because age is a significant risk factor for endometrial cancer; ultrasound findings do not replace the biopsy, and a hormonal trial before sampling treats an undiagnosed cause
  12. 44-year-old woman has 3 months of pelvic pressure and urinary frequency Regular, moderate periods; no further pregnancies planned uterus enlarged to 18 weeks' size, irregular BP 122/76 mm Hg · ultrasound shows moderate right hydronephrosis → Surgical management → bulk symptoms with hydronephrosis make the fibroids symptomatic, so they are treated surgically. Observation is for fibroids with no consequence, and the levonorgestrel device does not significantly shrink fibroids
  13. 32-year-old woman has had three first-trimester pregnancy losses Regular, heavy periods; wants to conceive Karyotypes normal in both partners saline infusion sonography: 2-cm fibroid projecting into the cavity hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Hysteroscopic myomectomy → a submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity raises spontaneous abortion rates; hysteroscopic myomectomy resects it and keeps the uterus. Uterine artery embolization is not ideal when she desires future fertility, and hysterectomy ends it
  14. 41-year-old woman is scheduled for myomectomy in 3 months Heavy periods from a 9-cm intramural fibroid Taking oral iron; wants a smaller uterus before surgery hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · ferritin 6 ng/mL · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Short-term GnRH agonist → a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist gives short-term relief until surgery: it reduces menstrual blood loss, typically inducing amenorrhea, so iron can rebuild the hemoglobin (preoperative hemoglobin rose by an average of 0.88 g/dL), and it decreases uterine volume. Monotherapy is limited to 6 months or less because bone mineral density falls with longer use; beyond 6 months, add-back estrogen and progestin. Tranexamic acid reduces bleeding but has not been shown to shrink fibroids
  15. 34-year-old woman has heavy, regular periods from small intramural fibroids Declines hormonal treatment; hopes to conceive next year cavity normal on ultrasound hemoglobin 11.0 g/dL · BP 120/76 mm Hg · urine pregnancy test negative → Tranexamic acid → oral tranexamic acid is nonhormonal and preserves fertility; it reduces bleeding without shrinking the fibroids. The combined pill and the levonorgestrel device are both hormonal, which she declines
  16. 45-year-old woman has 2 years of heavy, increasingly painful periods Three vaginal deliveries No pain with intercourse or bowel movements uterus uniformly enlarged, globular, boggy and tender Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL · urine pregnancy test negative → Adenomyosis → a globular, symmetric, boggy, tender uterus with severe dysmenorrhea; MRI shows a thickened junctional zone. Treat with a levonorgestrel intrauterine device or hysterectomy. A leiomyoma makes the uterus irregular, firm and lumpy. Endometriosis can bring dyspareunia and dyschezia, and the exam may show reduced uterine mobility or uterosacral nodularity
  17. 46-year-old woman has severe heavy periods and pelvic pressure from multiple fibroids Childbearing complete; wants definitive treatment Failed a year of medical therapy Benign endometrial biopsy uterus enlarged to 16 weeks' size hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Hysterectomy → with childbearing complete, severe symptoms and failed medical therapy, hysterectomy is the definitive option. After embolization as many as 19 to 38% undergo reintervention, and after myomectomy many need later procedures for recurrent fibroids
  18. 36-year-old woman has 6 hours of sudden severe left pelvic pain Known 6-cm pedunculated fibroid on the uterine surface tender mass contiguous with the uterus; ovaries normal on ultrasound T 37.8 °C · HR 104/min · urine pregnancy test negative → Torsion or degeneration of the fibroid → a pedunculated subserosal fibroid can torse, and fibroids can degenerate and hemorrhage; image it
  19. 62-year-old woman has 3 months of vaginal bleeding and pelvic fullness Menopause at 51; no hormone therapy uterus enlarged to 16 weeks' size; normal size 1 year ago hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · BP 134/82 mm Hg → Leiomyosarcoma → fibroids regress after menopause, so any growth after menopause, with bleeding and a rapidly enlarging uterus, is a sarcoma concern; it does not arise from a leiomyoma. Work it up without morcellation
  20. 58-year-old woman has 2 days of light vaginal spotting Last menstrual period 18 months ago No hormone therapy; no anticoagulants pale vaginal mucosa with minimal rugation BP 132/80 mm Hg · body mass index 24 kg/m² → Transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial biopsy → no period for over a year means she is postmenopausal. Postmenopausal bleeding usually is caused by atrophic changes of the vagina or endometrium, about 60%, but atrophy is a diagnosis of exclusion: the endometrium is evaluated first, and with no higher-risk feature, transvaginal ultrasound or endometrial sampling is a reasonable first approach. The pale vagina does not justify estrogen and reassurance, and a Pap test does not sample the endometrium
  21. 58-year-old woman has a single episode of vaginal spotting Menopause 6 years ago; no hormone therapy transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 3 mm, uniform BP 126/78 mm Hg · body mass index 26 kg/m² → Atrophic endometrium → an endometrial thickness of 4 mm or less has a greater than 99% negative predictive value for endometrial cancer, so no further workup unless bleeding recurs. Persistent or recurrent bleeding needs histology regardless of thickness, because rare cancers (particularly type II) present under 3 mm
  22. 58-year-old woman has 1 week of light vaginal bleeding Menopause 5 years ago; no hormone therapy transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 8 mm BP 138/84 mm Hg · body mass index 36 kg/m² → Endometrial biopsy → a thickness over 4 mm in a woman with postmenopausal bleeding needs endometrial sampling, and obesity adds unopposed estrogen. Repeat imaging and reassurance leave a possible cancer unsampled
  23. 58-year-old woman has 2 months of recurrent vaginal bleeding Menopause 7 years ago Office endometrial biopsy 3 weeks ago: insufficient tissue transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 7 mm hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL · BP 130/80 mm Hg → Hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage → when blind sampling does not give a diagnosis and bleeding persists, hysteroscopy with dilation and curettage is warranted; it is the gold standard for diagnostic sampling. Reassurance is never the answer to persistent bleeding
  24. 58-year-old woman has 1 week of vaginal spotting Taking tamoxifen for 3 years after breast cancer Menopause 8 years ago pelvic exam: normal cervix, no vaginal lesion BP 124/76 mm Hg · body mass index 27 kg/m² → Proceed with full evaluation regardless → tamoxifen raises endometrial cancer risk, so any bleeding on current tamoxifen gets endometrial sampling, whatever the stripe. Attributing the bleeding to the drug, or stopping it and waiting, delays the diagnosis
  25. 58-year-old woman had light vaginal bleeding for one day last week Menopause 4 years ago; no hormone therapy No bleeding since; feels well BP 128/80 mm Hg · body mass index 31 kg/m² · Afebrile → Evaluate with endometrial sampling → amount and duration are irrelevant: a single day of spotting counts. Sample the endometrium; transvaginal ultrasound is a reasonable first alternative for an initial episode. Waiting to see whether it recurs or lasts a week skips the evaluation
Management
Treatment by situation
SituationTreatmentNotes
Acute heavy bleeding, unstable or bleeding heavilyHospitalize; without contraindications to estrogen, intravenous conjugated estrogen every 4 to 6 hours (25 mg, for 24 hours), or a monophasic combined pill (30 to 50 micrograms ethinyl estradiol) every 6 to 8 hours until bleeding stops, then a taper; tranexamic acid may be used; transfuseMaintenance: combined hormonal contraceptives, oral or injectable progestins, or a levonorgestrel IUD; iron for anemia
Heavy menses, stableLevonorgestrel IUD, more effective than other medical therapies (71 to 95% less blood loss); oral tranexamic acid or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs if nonhormonal is wanted; in a bleeding disorder, aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs only on a hematologist's recommendationHysterectomy is the most effective treatment overall
Symptomatic fibroidsLevonorgestrel IUD or tranexamic acid for bleeding (neither shrinks fibroids); hysteroscopic myomectomy for a submucosal fibroid; myomectomy when she wants to keep fertility (it typically preserves it, though many need later procedures); hysterectomy, the definitive option, when childbearing is completeGonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist before surgery, 6 months or less alone, add-back beyond; embolization is not ideal if she wants future fertility
Hyperplasia without atypiaProgestin, oral or by levonorgestrel IUDTypically hormonal therapy and/or curettage
Atypical hyperplasia or endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia (EIN)HysterectomyMany have a concurrent carcinoma (about 43% in one series)
Endometrial carcinomaTotal abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy (TAH-BSO) and surgical staging with nodal assessmentHysterectomy and comprehensive staging are the standard of care
The IUD pairing The copper IUD typically makes menses heavier and occasionally longer. The levonorgestrel IUD makes them lighter and is a legitimate treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding. Any IUD is contraindicated in bleeding of unknown origin, so evaluate first.
Endometrial cancer risk Risk factors are unopposed estrogen: obesity, nulliparity, late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen, granulosa cell tumor, Lynch syndrome. Combined oral contraceptives and multiparity are protective.
Common wrong answers Treat-the-number: impressive fibroid anatomy on a computed tomography (CT) report is not, by itself, clinical significance. Uniform-answer doubt: anovulation is normal at her age, yet anemia still gets treated. True-fact-wrong-slot: fibroids do cause bleeding, but in premenopausal women; after menopause they involute. A Pap test for postmenopausal bleeding does not sample the endometrium. A same-sex relationship does not lower cervical cancer risk, and screening is identical; it does mean low pregnancy risk, so the contraceptive benefit of a combined oral contraceptive or an IUD does not offset their risks.
Pairs with Part I Hereditary Polyposis Syndromes covers the hereditary colon cancer differential. In it, Lynch syndrome, the endometrial-cancer pedigree, is the polyp-poor row. Ask: is there an endometrial cancer in the family?
Transferable rule

Treat the consequences of a finding, not the finding itself. Physiology that is normal for her age settles the diagnosis, not the management: before reassuring, look for a consequence (anemia, growth failure or functional impairment). A benign rash such as miliaria has no consequence but a removable cause, so remove it; normal anovulation with anemia is treated; impressive fibroid anatomy with no consequence is observed. And before accepting a familiar benign explanation, check that the patient is still in the physiologic state where it applies.

Fever and Sepsis in the Newborn

neonatal sepsis, its mimics and the febrile infant to 60 days · a laboratory value decides when the temperature does not; every reliable negative closes a sourceIs a laboratory value the only sign, and which source remains?

DiagnosisWorkup by agePracticeManagement
Bottom line

Fever is unreliable in the first month: neonates with sepsis may be afebrile or hypothermic, so without fever the laboratory results decide. With fever, the age band sets the workup.

  • Early-onset sepsis: onset within 72 hours; organisms from the maternal genital tract: group B Streptococcus (GBS), Escherichia coli and Listeria.
  • Late-onset sepsis: onset 72 hours to 90 days; nosocomial organisms join: coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus aureus, and Candida in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.
  • Leukopenia: the total white blood cell count (WBC) predicts early-onset sepsis poorly, but a low count in a neonate with these signs is sepsis until proven otherwise; it reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis.
  • Paradoxical irritability: quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved, because handling stretches inflamed meninges: the meningeal sign of infancy.
  • Neonatal empiric coverage: ampicillin plus gentamicin: ampicillin for GBS and Listeria (cephalosporins miss Listeria), gentamicin for gram-negative organisms (cefotaxime may be added or substituted if gram-negative meningitis is suspected); ampicillin plus cefotaxime when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed; ceftriaxone is avoided.
Diagnosis
The irritable neonate: leukopenia separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Neonatal sepsis, can't missEarly onset within 72 hours, late onset after; maternal GBS or chorioamnionitis; subtle: poor feeding, temperature instability, apnea, tachycardiaLeukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift; the neonate who “doesn’t look right”
Neonatal abstinence syndrome (NAS)Maternal opioid use; onset 24 to 72 hoursHigh-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing, hyperactive Moro; normal WBC
Neonatal hypoglycemiaInfant of a diabetic mother, large or small for gestational age, pretermJitteriness, lethargy, seizures; glucose below 40 to 45 mg/dL
Neonatal thyrotoxicosisMaternal Graves disease, requiredTachycardia, irritability, exophthalmos, goiter
Inborn error of metabolismPoor feeding after protein or galactose, day 2 to 5Metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, a specific dietary trigger
The toxic febrile infant: where is the source?
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Bacterial meningitisAny age; infants show no neck signsParadoxical irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry
Intussusception6 to 36 months, ileocolic, often post-viralParoxysmal crying with pain-free intervals, sausage mass, currant-jelly stool
Urinary tract infectionThe commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infantsPositive leukocyte esterase or nitrite with pyuria
Bacterial gastroenteritisHigh fever with crampingBloody or mucoid stools, many per day, sick contacts
Viral respiratory infectionCough, congestion, coryzaRhinorrhea and cough
Occult bacteremia or pneumoniaFever with leukocytosis, no localizing signTachypnea with hypoxia or focal crackles, not fever-driven tachypnea alone
Workup by age
Practice
  1. 3-day-old girl born at term is irritable and refusing feeds No maternal drug use or thyroid disease no tremor, sneezing or high-pitched cry T 37.0 °C (normothermic) · HR 180/min · white blood cells 3,000/mm³ · glucose normal → Ampicillin and gentamicin → leukopenia is the one value that separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics: it reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis. Ampicillin covers group B Streptococcus and Listeria, and gentamicin the gram-negative organisms. Intravenous dextrose answers a low glucose, and morphine answers neonatal abstinence, which brings tremor with a normal count. The total white cell count predicts early-onset sepsis poorly on its own, but here it is the one abnormal value
  2. 7-month-old boy has fever and cries violently when picked up lies quietly when left undisturbed Three loose stools today; no cough or rhinorrhea T 39.5 °C · white blood cells 16,000/mm³ with 83% neutrophils · urine dipstick negative, specific gravity 1.030 → Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture → crying on being handled with calm when undisturbed is paradoxical irritability, the meningeal sign of infancy. No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch; a negative dipstick in concentrated urine closes the urinary branch. Three loose stools are a nonspecific systemic response and do not explain the paradoxical irritability, and paroxysmal crying with a mass would earn the ultrasound
  3. 2-day-old boy is jittery with a high-pitched cry Mother used heroin throughout the pregnancy frequent sneezing hyperactive Moro reflex T 37.1 °C · HR 164/min · white blood cells 12,000/mm³ · glucose normal → Neonatal abstinence syndrome → maternal opioid use with onset at 24 to 72 hours, a high-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing and a hyperactive Moro reflex with a normal white cell count; supportive care, considering morphine if severe. A normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia, and a normal count with a clear drug history argues against sepsis
  4. 9-month-old boy has episodes of crying with his legs drawn up Calm between episodes, but now lethargic Episodes began 6 hours ago and recur every 20 minutes sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass T 37.6 °C · HR 150/min → Abdominal ultrasound → paroxysmal crying with pain-free intervals and a sausage mass at 6 to 36 months: the ultrasound shows a target sign. Paroxysmal crying with calm intervals is the mirror of the constant paradoxical irritability that earns a lumbar puncture
  5. 1-day-old girl is jittery and lethargic Mother had gestational diabetes large for gestational age Born at 39 weeks by cesarean delivery; Apgar scores 8 and 9 T 36.8 °C · HR 150/min · glucose 28 mg/dL → Intravenous dextrose infusion → an infant of a diabetic mother with jitteriness, lethargy and a glucose below 40 to 45 mg/dL is symptomatic hypoglycemia, treated with intravenous dextrose. Antibiotics answer leukopenia, not a low glucose, and observation leaves a symptomatic infant untreated
  6. 8-month-old girl has fever with no localizing findings No cough, rhinorrhea or diarrhea Immunizations are up to date; fever began 2 days ago catheterized urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase T 39.2 °C · HR 160/min → Urine culture and empiric antibiotics → the commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infants: a positive dipstick sends the urine for culture and starts antibiotics. A lumbar puncture tests the wrong fluid without a meningeal sign, and observation leaves a likely infection untreated
  7. 4-day-old girl has tachycardia and tremor Mother has Graves disease; no maternal drug use Born at 38 weeks poor weight gain since birth exophthalmos warm, moist skin T 37.4 °C · HR 196/min · white blood cells 9,000/mm³ → Neonatal thyrotoxicosis → maternal Graves disease with tachycardia, tremor and exophthalmos; free thyroxine is high and thyroid-stimulating hormone low, and propranolol with methimazole treats it. Neonatal abstinence needs a maternal drug history
  8. 21-day-old boy has fever, irritability and poor feeding bulging anterior fontanelle irritable when handled Born at term; discharged home on day 2; no sick contacts Feeding half his usual volume T 38.8 °C · HR 188/min → Lumbar puncture with blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus cefotaxime → a previously well infant from home has community-acquired late-onset disease, treated like early-onset disease, and a bulging fontanelle is a meningitis concern: ampicillin covers Listeria, which cephalosporins do not, and cefotaxime replaces gentamicin when meningitis is strongly suspected because it achieves superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration; the lumbar puncture decides whether this is meningitis and so the length of treatment. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin leaves Listeria uncovered, and observation misses a bulging fontanelle
  9. 7-month-old boy has a rash on his trunk Fever to 39 °C for 3 days ended yesterday blanching rose-pink macules on the trunk playful and well appearing T 37.0 °C · HR 120/min → Roseola infantum → high fever that breaks before a blanching rose-pink truncal rash appears is human herpesvirus 6; no testing is needed. In measles, fever may spike when the rash appears, and a well, playful infant has no meningeal sign
  10. 6-hour-old boy has grunting and nasal flaring Mother had chorioamnionitis during labor Born at 39 weeks after 20 hours of labor; Apgar scores 7 and 8 subcostal retractions HR 170/min · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 94% → Blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → maternal chorioamnionitis with early respiratory distress is early-onset infection until proven otherwise: draw cultures, but do not delay ampicillin with an aminoglycoside. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin is the right class at the wrong age, and observation delays treatment
  11. 10-month-old boy has fever and irritability bulging anterior fontanelle high-pitched cry Ill for one day, with two episodes of vomiting No rash; no pain-free intervals T 39.3 °C · HR 172/min → Bacterial meningitis → a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry are the infant's meningeal signs, since neck signs are unreliable; neuroimaging if signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as focal signs or papilledema, are present. Intussusception cries in paroxysms with calm intervals, and roseola brings a rash after the fever
  12. 5-day-old boy was diagnosed with sepsis yesterday Blood culture result pending Born at term; empiric antibiotics are being chosen jaundiced to the chest feeding poorly T 37.9 °C · HR 168/min · total bilirubin 14 mg/dL → Ceftriaxone → ceftriaxone displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract as sludge; it is contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates or with calcium-containing intravenous solutions. Ampicillin and gentamicin are the neonatal regimen
  13. 6-month-old boy has fever and cries whenever he is held bulging anterior fontanelle The lumbar puncture will be delayed an hour T 39.4 °C · HR 176/min · BP 84/50 mm Hg → Give empiric antibiotics now and perform the lumbar puncture after → if the tap is delayed, give antibiotics first: a sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable trade. Waiting, or deferring antibiotics until cultures return, delays treatment
  14. 1-day-old boy born at 39 weeks has grunting and poor feeding Mother had a fever in labor; no intrapartum antibiotics Membranes ruptured 20 hours before delivery lethargic T 38.4 °C · HR 182/min · blood culture pending → Group B Streptococcus → early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract, and in a term infant group B Streptococcus leads; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis prevents early-onset disease. Escherichia coli now predominates among preterm and very low birth weight neonates, and Listeria is the organism ampicillin is kept for
  15. 12-month-old girl has fever and vomiting papilledema on funduscopy; anterior fontanelle closed new weakness of the right arm and leg Empiric intravenous antibiotics have been given T 39.6 °C · HR 168/min · BP 96/58 mm Hg → Head CT before lumbar puncture → papilledema or a focal deficit puts imaging before the tap, and antibiotics come first, then CT, then the lumbar puncture if imaging shows it is safe. An immediate tap is premature: signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal neurologic signs are reasons the tap may be delayed, and waiting for blood culture results holds up imaging that belongs during or right after the antibiotics
  16. 21-day-old girl born at 39 weeks has a fever Well appearing and feeding normally Parents measured the fever an hour ago; no sick contacts no rash, cough or focal findings T 38.4 °C rectal · HR 168/min → Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics → at 8 to 21 days the AAP guideline calls for a catheterized urinalysis, a blood culture and cerebrospinal fluid, parenteral antibiotics and hospital monitoring, even when the infant looks well. A urine-only workup or discharge without cerebrospinal fluid falls short in this band
  17. 8-month-old boy has fever, petechiae and lethargy Ill for 12 hours; capillary refill 5 seconds A lumbar puncture tray is being prepared T 39.8 °C · HR 190/min · BP 64/30 mm Hg → Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture → treat first, tap after: in shock with petechiae, a lumbar puncture never delays antibiotics. Blood cultures are right as long as they do not delay the first dose, and intravenous fluid boluses are suggested for the shock
Management
Empiric antibiotics by age Neonate (0 to 28 days) – ampicillin plus gentamicin, covering GBS, E. coli and Listeria; cefotaxime may be added to or substituted for the gentamicin if gram-negative meningitis is suspected, and ampicillin plus cefotaxime is preferred when meningitis is strongly suspected or confirmed, for its superior cerebrospinal fluid penetration. The 2021 AAP table lists ampicillin with ceftazidime or gentamicin for 8 to 28 days. Where extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing E. coli circulates, gentamicin replaces ceftazidime for suspected bacteremia or sepsis, and meropenem replaces it when meningitis is suspected · 29 to 60 days – ceftriaxone, with vancomycin added when bacteremia or meningitis is a concern; the neonatal organisms recede and ceftriaxone’s biliary risk becomes acceptable · Ceftriaxone in a neonate – avoided: it displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract as sludge; contraindicated in hyperbilirubinemic neonates or with calcium-containing intravenous solutions · Herpes simplex virus (HSV) risk – maternal genital HSV lesions or fever 48 hours before or after delivery; vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis with a negative Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or raised transaminases: acyclovir joins the parenteral antibiotics
Sequence and its exceptions With focal deficits or papilledema, give antibiotics first, obtain neuroimaging during or right after them, then tap if imaging shows it is safe. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended: the fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so, without signs of raised intracranial pressure, tap without imaging first. If the tap will be delayed, give antibiotics first. Draw the blood culture, but never let it delay antibiotics.
8 to 21 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: catheter or suprapubic aspiration specimen for urinalysis, and for culture if the urinalysis is positive
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersMay assess
CSFShould obtain for cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain and bacterial culture
AntibioticsShould start parenteral therapy
WhereShould actively monitor in hospital, with staff experienced with neonates, while cultures are pending
StopShould stop parenteral antibiotics and discharge when cultures are negative for 24 to 36 hours (or grow only contaminants), the infant still appears well or is improving, and no other reason for hospitalization remains. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered with maternal genital HSV lesions or fever from 48 hours before to 48 hours after delivery, or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase; then parenteral antibiotics including acyclovir
22 to 28 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: catheter or suprapubic specimen for urinalysis and culture if positive, or a bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersShould assess
CSFShould obtain if any marker is abnormal. May obtain even if no marker is abnormal (urinalysis negative or positive), once blood and urine cultures are taken and the infant is hospitalized
Antibiotics, hospitalShould give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis or the urinalysis is positive. May give it if CSF and urinalysis are normal but a marker is abnormal, and may even if the urinalysis and all markers are normal and CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive
Antibiotics, homeShould give parenteral therapy before home management, even if the urinalysis, all markers and CSF are normal
HomeMay manage at home if the urinalysis and all markers are normal, CSF is normal or enterovirus-positive, verbal and written instructions are given, a recheck in 24 hours is arranged, and plans for a change in condition (contact with providers, access to emergency care) are in place
HospitalShould admit if CSF is not obtained or is uninterpretable
StopShould stop antibiotics and discharge hospitalized infants after 24 to 36 hours of negative cultures if the infant is well or improving, with no other reason for hospitalization and no other infection needing treatment (such as otitis media). At home, should stop when the infant is well or improving at reassessment, all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and no other infection needs treatment. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered (HSV can occur in this age group) with vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase
29 to 60 days (AAP 2021)
DecisionAction and condition
UrineShould: bag or voided specimen for urinalysis with a catheter or suprapubic culture if positive, or a catheter or suprapubic specimen for both
Blood cultureShould obtain
Inflammatory markersShould assess
CSFNeed not obtain if all markers are normal. May obtain if any marker is abnormal, testing for enterovirus when pleocytosis is found or in enterovirus season
AntibioticsShould give parenteral therapy if CSF suggests bacterial meningitis. May give it if CSF (if obtained) is normal and any marker is abnormal. Should start oral therapy if the urinalysis is positive, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal. Need not give any while cultures are pending if the urinalysis is negative, no marker is abnormal and CSF (if obtained) is normal or enterovirus-positive
HospitalShould admit if CSF (if obtained) is abnormal. May admit if any marker is abnormal
HomeShould manage at home if CSF (if obtained) is normal, the urinalysis is negative and all markers are normal, with parental education, a recheck in 24 hours and plans for a change in condition. May manage at home without antibiotics or interpretable CSF if the urinalysis is negative, all markers are normal and parents can return promptly and agree to follow-up in 24 to 36 hours; reassess within 24 hours
StopShould stop antibiotics when all cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours, the infant is well or improving and no other infection needs treatment. With a positive urine culture, should discharge if blood and CSF (if obtained) cultures are negative, the infant is well or improving and no other reason for hospitalization remains; at home, should stop parenteral antibiotics (if started) and begin or continue oral therapy when other cultures are negative at 24 to 36 hours and the infant is well or improving. Should treat a positive culture with targeted therapy for a duration fitting the disease, organism and response
HSVShould be considered, although uncommon, with maternal genital HSV lesions or vesicles, seizures, hypothermia, mucous membrane ulcers, pleocytosis without a positive Gram stain, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia or a raised alanine aminotransferase
Organisms and prevention Early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract: GBS, E. coli (often carrying the K1 (capsular antigen 1) capsule) and Listeria. Intrapartum penicillin prophylaxis reduced early-onset GBS disease but did not change E. coli rates, and E. coli now predominates among preterm and VLBW neonates. No strategy yet prevents late-onset GBS disease, and its rate is unchanged. GBS remains a leading cause of meningitis and bloodstream infection under 3 months. For GBS disease the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) counts early onset as under 7 days and late onset as 7 to 89 days.
Reading the febrile infant Fever without a source is documented fever with no localizing findings after history and examination. Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry. A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out: leukocyte esterase is about 83% sensitive and nitrite about 53%, because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction; both negative in concentrated urine (specific gravity 1.030) is genuinely reassuring. Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localizing findings. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, do a lumbar puncture. Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis. In the first days, 5% weight loss at day 3 is physiologic (up to 7 to 10% in breastfed newborns).
Common wrong answers Neonatal abstinence or hypoglycemia for an irritable, poorly feeding neonate: either fits the behavior, but leukopenia fits neither. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin under 29 days: the right class of empiric coverage at the wrong age. Propranolol: it treats neonatal thyrotoxicosis, which does not produce leukopenia. Abdominal ultrasound for paradoxical irritability: intussusception is the other inconsolable infant, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals. Urine culture with a meningeal sign: the right class of test on the wrong fluid. Stool testing: three loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 °C with 83% neutrophils.
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF grid and the neonatal organism-by-host list, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Ask: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Aquifer Fever in an Infant covers which tests the age, appearance and vaccines call for, and the febrile urinary tract infection that is most often found.
Transferable rule

In a neonate the absence of fever does not exclude sepsis: without fever and with no maternal drug history, the WBC decides, not the behavioral pattern. In a febrile infant, name the disease first by elimination, then choose the test that follows from it; each reliable negative finding closes a source, and the diagnosis is the source that remains.

Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications

contraindication, precaution or neither for DTaP (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis) · which vaccines a well infant's age allows at this visitHas the vaccine's age window opened, or closed, and can you name the criterion that makes this child ineligible?

Contraindication or notInfant visitsPractice
Bottom line

Two checks at every vaccine visit: has the child's age opened the vaccine's window, and has the window closed? Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes this child ineligible; a history that only sounds disqualifying is not one.

  • Contraindication: never give. For DTaP: anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component; or encephalopathy (coma, decreased consciousness, prolonged seizures) within 7 days of a previous dose with no other cause. Encephalopathy is a contraindication to pertussis vaccine only, so finish the series with DT (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids).
  • Precaution: weigh risk against benefit. In general defer; vaccination may be indicated when the benefit outweighs the risk, as in an outbreak.
  • Neither: vaccinate today.
  • Up to date at 4 months: the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due: DTaP, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine), IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine) and oral rotavirus.
Contraindication, precaution or neither
DTaP: contraindications, precautions and histories that are neither
CategoryHistories
Contraindication
(every pertussis-containing vaccine)		Anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component · Encephalopathy within 7 days of a previous dose, not due to another cause: give DT instead
Precaution
(defer or weigh)		Progressive or unstable neurologic disorder: infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy, progressive encephalopathy; defer until neurologic status is clarified and stable · Guillain-Barré syndrome within 6 weeks of a previous tetanus-toxoid dose · Arthus-type reaction to a previous diphtheria- or tetanus-toxoid dose; defer until at least 10 years after the last tetanus-toxoid dose · Moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever
NeitherAfter a previous dose: fever of 40.5 °C or higher within 48 hours, a hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode (collapse or shock-like state) within 48 hours, a seizure within 3 days, or inconsolable crying for 3 hours or more within 48 hours · Family history of seizures or epilepsy · Stable or resolved neurologic conditions · Personal febrile seizure · Mild illness · Recent exposure
Older sources differ Older sources, including the earlier version of this brief, list those four post-dose reactions as precautions. The CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) now lists them as conditions incorrectly perceived as contraindications or precautions.
Vaccines at the infant visits
Vaccines due at each infant visit
VisitVaccines dueAge limit that matters
2 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, first doses; hepatitis B second dose if not given at 1 monthRotavirus must start by 14 weeks 6 days
4 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, second dosesToo young for influenza (6 months) and for MMR and varicella (12 months)
6 monthsDTaP and PCV third doses; Hib third dose except with PedvaxHIB; rotavirus third dose with RV5 only; IPV and hepatitis B third doses (due 6 to 18 months); influenza in seasonRotavirus series ends by 8 months 0 days; the first influenza season needs 2 doses
12 to 15 monthsMMR and varicella first doses; hepatitis A first of 2 doses (12 to 23 months); PCV fourth dose; Hib boosterRoutine MMR and varicella start at 12 months
Schedule status, October 2026 In January 2026 the CDC moved childhood rotavirus and influenza vaccines from routine to shared clinical decision-making. A federal court stayed that change in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts is the 2025 schedule, which lists both vaccines as routine; check the CDC site for the current schedule. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) publishes its own schedule and opposed the change, and the NBME item keys rotavirus as a routine 4-month vaccine.
Practice
  1. 2-month-old boy is at the well-child visit for his first vaccines His father has epilepsy, and an older sister had seizures with fever His mother asks to skip the pertussis vaccine development and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 140/min → Neither → a family history of seizures or epilepsy is neither a contraindication nor a precaution: vaccinate today. The mother's request is a matter for counseling; it does not change the classification
  2. 6-month-old boy is brought for his third DTaP dose Two days after his 4-month dose he was hard to arouse and had a prolonged seizure Evaluation found no other cause T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min alert and interactive today → Contraindication → decreased consciousness and a prolonged seizure within 7 days of a previous dose, with no other cause, is the encephalopathy that contraindicates every pertussis-containing vaccine: complete the series with DT. A precaution is weighed; this is not
  3. 17-week-old boy is starting his infant vaccines today His family moved from another state He received only the hepatitis B birth dose growth and examination normal T 36.9 °C · HR 138/min → Rotavirus vaccine → the rotavirus series cannot start on or after 15 weeks 0 days (first dose by 14 weeks 6 days), so it is never given to him. DTaP and the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine are 2-month vaccines he is due for
  4. 4-month-old girl is due for her 4-month vaccines Runny nose and mild cough for 2 days; feeding well playful; clear nasal discharge; lungs clear T 38.1 °C · HR 150/min · respirations 40/min → Neither → a mild acute illness, with or without fever, is neither: vaccinate today. Moderate or severe acute illness is the precaution
  5. 12-month-old boy is at his well-child visit with his mother She is 20 weeks pregnant and asks whether his vaccines could harm the fetus Healthy; up to date on infant vaccines examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 118/min → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella vaccines today → the CDC lists pregnancy of the recipient's mother or another close or household contact as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution for both vaccines. Pregnancy contraindicates them only in the person being vaccinated, so neither is deferred
  6. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose Clusters of sudden flexion spasms began 3 weeks ago and continue daily despite treatment She has lost the ability to roll over T 36.8 °C · HR 122/min → Precaution → infantile spasms are a progressive neurologic disorder: a precaution, so defer DTaP until neurologic status is clarified and stable. A brief seizure within 3 days of a dose, or a stable neurologic condition, would be neither
  7. 7-month-old girl is at a well-child visit in November Up to date on her infant vaccines She has never received influenza vaccine growth and examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 130/min → Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeks → influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, every season; a child aged 6 months to 8 years with fewer than 2 earlier doses, or an unknown history, gets 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart. Waiting for the 12-month visit misses this season
  8. 6-month-old girl is brought for her third DTaP dose The night after her 4-month dose her temperature reached 41 °C; it resolved within a day No seizure; well since then T 36.7 °C · HR 125/min → Neither → fever of 40.5 °C or higher within 48 hours of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution
  9. 12-month-old girl returns 2 weeks after her 12-month visit She received measles-mumps-rubella vaccine at that visit; varicella vaccine was out of stock Healthy; no immune problems examination normal T 36.8 °C · HR 120/min → Varicella vaccine in 2 weeks → injected live vaccines not given on the same day need at least 4 weeks between them; varicella vaccine given today, 2 weeks after measles-mumps-rubella vaccine, would not count and would have to be repeated at least 4 weeks later. Waiting until 4 to 6 years skips the first varicella dose, due at 12 to 15 months
  10. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Within 10 minutes of her 2-month dose she developed hives, wheezing and low blood pressure She received epinephrine in the clinic T 37.0 °C · HR 132/min → Contraindication → hives, wheezing and hypotension within minutes of a dose is anaphylaxis: a severe allergic reaction after a previous dose or to a vaccine component contraindicates that vaccine
  11. 12-month-old boy is at a well-child visit Up to date on his vaccines, including the rotavirus series Healthy, with normal growth and development examination normal; no immune problems T 36.7 °C · HR 118/min → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella → MMR and varicella are the live injected vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months, with second doses at 4 to 6 years; the rotavirus series ended by 8 months 0 days
  12. 4-month-old girl is brought for her second DTaP dose Six hours after her 2-month dose she had a brief seizure that stopped on its own Since then she has been well, with normal development T 37.0 °C · HR 135/min → Neither → a seizure within 3 days of a previous dose is listed by the CDC as a condition incorrectly perceived as a contraindication or precaution: vaccinate today. Older sources called it a precaution. Uncontrolled seizures or a progressive neurologic disorder would be the precaution
  13. 4-month-old boy is due for his 4-month vaccines Admitted yesterday with pneumonia; needs supplemental oxygen tachypneic with right-sided crackles T 39.2 °C · HR 170/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air → Precaution → a moderate or severe acute illness, with or without fever, is a precaution: in general defer until he recovers. A mild illness, such as a cold with low fever, is neither
How NBME framed it: question 1

4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October Uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; vaccines up to date Normal growth and development for age vital signs normal normal examination

Immunization against which disease is most appropriate at this time?

Competing answers
  • Chickenpox: a routine live childhood vaccine; but the first varicella dose is not given until 12 months.
  • Measles-mumps-rubella: routine and live, like rotavirus; but the first dose is at 12 months.
  • Shingles: the same virus as chickenpox; but zoster vaccine is for adults from age 50; the NBME explanation, an older source, says 60.

Down to two: rotavirus or influenza. Rotavirus: up to date at 4 months means the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due, rotavirus among them. The October date is a seasonal cue for influenza, but at 4 months she is below its 6-month age limit. The options form an age ladder, from rotavirus at 2 months through MMR and varicella at 12 months to zoster at 50.

Not a reason to withhold routine childhood vaccines Mild illness, with or without fever · current antibiotic therapy · preterm birth: vaccinate at chronological age, full dose (hepatitis B vaccine is an exception in certain circumstances: deferred under 2,000 g if the mother is documented to be hepatitis B surface antigen negative) · breastfeeding · family history of allergies; family history of seizures or a vaccine reaction (for DTaP) · recent exposure to an infectious disease · penicillin allergy · egg allergy: any influenza vaccine appropriate for age · pregnancy or immunosuppression in a household contact; a caregiver of a severely immunosuppressed person in a protective environment should not get LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine); smallpox vaccine is the exception: close household contacts are screened for its contraindications · mild local reaction (redness or swelling at the injection site) to a previous dose.
Which childhood vaccines are live
ClassVaccines
Live attenuatedRotavirus · measles · mumps · rubella · varicella; also LAIV, BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin), oral polio and live zoster vaccine (no longer available in the United States since 2020)
Inactivated (killed)Polio · hepatitis A · injectable influenza
ToxoidDiphtheria · tetanus
Subunit or conjugateHepatitis B · pertussis · Hib · pneumococcal · meningococcal · HPV (human papillomavirus)
Schedule and timing DTaP at 2, 4 and 6 months, 15 to 18 months and 4 to 6 years · Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis booster) at 11 to 12 years and in every pregnancy, preferably early in weeks 27 to 36 · pertussis postexposure prophylaxis for household contacts within 21 days of the index patient's cough onset · live injected or nasal vaccines on the same day or at least 4 weeks apart · after IVIG (intravenous immune globulin) or blood products, defer MMR and varicella 3 to 11 months, by product.
Rotavirus and zoster Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral: do not give it with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) or after an intussusception. Recombinant zoster vaccine is 2 doses 2 to 6 months apart from age 50, or from age 19 with immunocompromise; older sources, including the NBME explanation, start zoster vaccine at 60.
Pairs with Aquifer Adolescent Vaccines covers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season. Ask: has this child reached the vaccine's age window, and has the window closed?
Transferable rule

Check the child's age against each vaccine's age window before the season or the disease; a vaccine whose window has not opened, or has closed, is not given at this visit. Then vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes the child ineligible.
