Rashes in the Newborn and Infant

benign newborn rashes sorted by onset, then the diaper rash split by its folds · reassure, remove a cause, or treat what was addedHow old is the baby, is there a removable cause or a red flag, and does the diaper rash involve the creases?

DiagnosisPracticeManagement
Bottom line

Reassure when a benign, self-limited rash has no modifiable cause; remove the trigger when it has an identifiable, removable one. Sort by onset age first. A rash outside its window, erythema toxicum-like pustules on the palms or soles, vesicles or crusting, or a febrile or irritable infant is not benign until the dangerous mimics are excluded. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex virus (HSV) until proven otherwise: polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing and IV acyclovir.

  • Erythema toxicum neonatorum: firm yellow-white pustules on a blotchy red base, on the face, trunk and proximal limbs; palms and soles usually spared; a well infant. The diagnosis is usually clinical; a smear, rarely needed, shows eosinophils.
  • Transient neonatal pustular melanosis: pustules without surrounding erythema that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; may involve the palms and soles; more common in darker skin; neutrophils.
  • Milia: firm pearly white papules on the nose and cheeks, no erythema; retained keratin.
  • Miliaria rubra: blocked sweat glands; fine red papules and vesicles on occluded, covered and intertriginous skin (neck, axillae, groin). Its cause is in the history (a onesie under pajamas under a fleece swaddle), so treat it by unwrapping the baby, not by waiting it out. Superficial 1- to 2-mm vesicles are miliaria crystallina, usually before 2 weeks; the HSV rule still applies until herpes is excluded.
  • Neonatal cephalic pustulosis: red papules and pustules on the face and scalp only; no comedones, unlike true neonatal acne (closed comedones); linked to Malassezia.
  • Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy yellow scale on the scalp (cradle cap), with redness in the folds; usually not itchy, and the infant looks content.
  • Diaper rash: irritant contact dermatitis, the most common, sits on the convex skin the wet diaper touches and usually spares the creases; Candida involves the creases, with satellite papules. A rash that got better on a barrier and then got worse has acquired something the barrier does not treat.
Diagnosis
Diaper rash: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tell
Candidal diaper dermatitisYeast, on its own or on top of irritation; after diarrhea or antibiotics, or with thrush; the second most common diaper rashBeefy-red plaques in the creases with satellite papules; worse despite the barrier
Irritant contact dermatitisUrine and stool on convex skin; the commonest diaper rashUsually spares the creases; no satellites; responds to a barrier
Perianal group A streptococcal diseaseBacterial; painful defecation and stool withholdingBright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash, with or without anal fissures
ScabiesMite; refractory diaper rash in an infant with itchy contactsDiffuse: trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles
Acrodermatitis enteropathicaZinc deficiency; rare and refractoryChronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopecia
Sexually transmitted infection, can't missThe concern behind any genital rashVerrucous papules of human papillomavirus, ulcers with fever and adenopathy of HSV, or mucopurulent discharge of gonorrhea and chlamydia
Practice
  1. 2-day-old boy has a blotchy rash noticed this morning Breastfeeding well; born at term after an uncomplicated delivery red macules with central yellow-white pustules on trunk and proximal limbs palms and soles spared Afebrile · HR 136/min · well appearing → Erythema toxicum neonatorum → firm yellow-white pustules on a blotchy red base over the trunk and proximal limbs, sparing the palms and soles, in a well 2-day-old: a clinical diagnosis that needs only reassurance. Neonatal herpes brings clustered vesicles on a red base, and staphylococcal pustulosis brings honey-colored crusts in the diaper area or at a wound
  2. 2-week-old boy has had a rash on his neck and chest for 2 days Dressed in a onesie, pajamas and a fleece swaddle tiny red papules on the neck and upper chest; no pustules or vesicles Afebrile · well appearing → Miliaria rubra → small red papules on covered skin under three layers are blocked sweat ducts, so remove the extra layers. Vesicles of any kind in a neonate would first need herpes simplex excluded. Erythema toxicum appears in the first days as pustules on a blotchy red base, and neonatal acne brings closed comedones on the face
  3. 1-day-old boy has spots that were present at birth Born at term; breastfeeding well small pustules without surrounding redness on chin, neck and back some ruptured, leaving brown macules with a collarette of scale Afebrile · well appearing → Transient neonatal pustular melanosis → pustules present at birth, without surrounding erythema, that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; a smear would show neutrophils. Reassure: the pustules clear in days and the pigment fades over weeks to months. Erythema toxicum pustules sit on a red base, and congenital syphilis is a maculopapular rash with no pustules
  4. 2-week-old boy has been irritable and feeding poorly for 1 day a cluster of vesicles on a red base on the scalp Born vaginally at term; no rash before yesterday T 37.9 °C · HR 172/min → Neonatal herpes simplex → clustered vesicles on a red base in an irritable 2-week-old: any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex until proven otherwise, so send PCR and start IV acyclovir. Erythema toxicum appears in the first days in a well baby, and miliaria rubra follows overbundling
  5. 1-day-old girl is examined before discharge Born at term; feeding well; mother asks about bumps on the nose 1-mm firm pearly white papules across the nose and cheeks no surrounding redness; no pustules Afebrile · HR 140/min → Milia → pearly white papules of retained keratin on the nose and cheeks with no erythema, present at birth: reassure; they usually clear within the first month and may persist into the second or third month; do not extract them. Cephalic pustulosis brings red papules and pustules from about the third week, and miliaria rubra red papules on covered skin
  6. 6-week-old boy has had scaling on his scalp for 3 weeks greasy yellow scale over the crown mild redness in the neck creases Not scratching; content and feeding well Afebrile · weight gain normal → Seborrheic dermatitis → greasy yellow scale on the scalp with redness in the folds in a content infant: reassure; it is self-limited, and an emollient with gentle brushing can loosen the scale. Atopic dermatitis is the main differential; this rash is usually not itchy. Tinea capitis brings patchy hair loss
  7. 3-week-old girl has had a rash on her neck and underarms for 2 days Kept in a fleece swaddle over footed pajamas in a warm room fine red papules in the neck folds and axillae Afebrile · feeding well · well appearing → Lighter, cooler clothing → blocked sweat ducts under too many layers in a warm room: the cause is in the history, so remove it with thin cotton, a cool room and no overbundling. Nystatin treats yeast in the diaper creases, and reassurance without changes leaves the cause in place
  8. 10-day-old girl has a cluster of blisters on her scalp vesicles grouped on a red base, 1 cm across Born vaginally at term; feeding well; no other skin lesions Afebrile · HR 150/min · alert → HSV PCR and IV acyclovir → any vesicular rash in a neonate is herpes simplex virus until proven otherwise, even in a well, afebrile baby: send HSV PCR and start IV acyclovir. Reassurance misses an infection that can disseminate, and mupirocin treats the honey-crusted pustules of staphylococcal pustulosis
  9. 4-month-old boy has had a diaper rash for 5 days beefy-red plaques involving the inguinal creases satellite papules beyond the border No new soaps or wipes; stools normal Afebrile · well appearing → Topical nystatin → creases involved, with satellite papules, is Candida: a topical antifungal such as nystatin, applied with every diaper change, under the barrier. Zinc oxide alone treats irritant dermatitis, which usually spares the creases, and a steroid does not treat the yeast
  10. 4-month-old girl is seen for a well-child visit flat blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks Present since birth, her parents say; no other skin findings Growing and developing normally Afebrile · HR 128/min → Document the finding and reassure → blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, are benign and self-resolving by age 3 to 5 years; documenting them prevents confusion with non-accidental trauma. A skeletal survey and a report are for injuries, not birthmarks
  11. 3-day-old boy has a rash noted at his newborn check Breastfeeding well; mother had a cold sore last year yellow-white pustules on blotchy red bases, face and trunk palms, soles spared; no vesicles T 37.0 °C · well appearing → Reassurance only → pustules on a red base over the face and trunk, sparing the palms and soles, in a well newborn: reassure; they fade over 5 to 7 days and may recur for several weeks. A maternal cold sore does not make this herpes: neonatal HSV usually brings clustered vesicles; those without them usually have eye, mouth or central nervous system disease, and these are pustules on a red base in a well newborn; base the diagnosis on the morphology and the baby's well appearance. Congenital syphilis is maculopapular, includes the palms and soles and has no pustules
  12. 3-week-old girl has had bumps on her face for 4 days red papules and pustules on cheeks, forehead and scalp no comedones Trunk, palms and soles clear; feeding well Afebrile · well appearing → Neonatal cephalic pustulosis → red papules and pustules confined to the face and scalp, often from the third week, with no comedones, linked to Malassezia: observe; it generally resolves without treatment over weeks to months, and if the look bothers the parents, a topical antifungal such as ketoconazole can be used safely and may help. Erythema toxicum peaks in the first days and involves the trunk; miliaria rubra favors covered skin
  13. 6-day-old boy has sores at his circumcision site Circumcised on day 2; feeding well a few pustules and flaccid blisters around the site some ruptured to honey-colored crusts; skin elsewhere normal Afebrile · HR 140/min → Topical mupirocin → localized pustules and flaccid blisters that rupture to honey-colored crusts at a wound are staphylococcal pustulosis: topical mupirocin. Reassurance leaves a bacterial infection untreated, and acyclovir is for clustered vesicles on a red base
  14. 14-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 10 days It faded on zinc oxide paste, then spread over 3 days Gastroenteritis last week, now resolved beefy-red plaques into the inguinal folds with satellite papules Afebrile · playful → Topical nystatin under the barrier → a rash that improved on barrier therapy and then worsened has acquired something the barrier does not treat; creases and satellites name Candida, seeded after the diarrhea. Add a topical antifungal under the barrier, not instead of it. Topical agents are preferred for superficial infection, so oral fluconazole is not the step
  15. 8-month-old boy has had a red diaper rash for 2 days mild erythematous papules and plaques over the buttocks and thighs inguinal creases spared; no satellite lesions Eating and sleeping normally Afebrile · well appearing → Barrier ointment with more frequent diaper changes → convex skin involved and creases spared, with no satellites, is irritant contact dermatitis, the most common diaper rash: a barrier such as zinc oxide or petrolatum and frequent changes. Nystatin is for yeast in the creases, and a short course of a low-potency steroid is for rashes that do not improve within 2 to 3 days, or moderate to severe cases
  16. 3-year-old girl has had pain with bowel movements for 1 week bright red, sharply demarcated perianal plaque a small anal fissure Withholding stool for 3 days; toilet trained Afebrile · abdomen soft → Oral amoxicillin → a bright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash with a fissure and painful defecation is perianal group A streptococcal disease: oral antibiotics such as amoxicillin. Nystatin treats yeast, and a barrier alone leaves the bacterial infection untreated
  17. 4-month-old boy has had a diaper rash for 3 days Taking amoxicillin for otitis media, day 6 of 10 beefy-red confluent rash in the inguinal creases white plaques on the buccal mucosa Afebrile · feeding well → Topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin → creases involved after antibiotics, with oral thrush, is yeast in both places: topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin for the mouth. Stopping the amoxicillin leaves the yeast untreated, and hydrocortisone does not treat it
  18. 5-month-old boy has a diaper rash that has not cleared with barrier cream papules also on the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles His mother itches at night Afebrile · well appearing → Scabies → a refractory diaper rash that also involves the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles, with an itchy household contact, is scabies: permethrin for the infant and all household contacts. Yeast and irritant dermatitis stay in the diaper area
  19. 7-month-old girl has had a perineal rash for 6 weeks despite treatment red, crusted plaques around the mouth and in the diaper area diffuse hair loss Chronic diarrhea for 2 months Afebrile · irritable → Acrodermatitis enteropathica → chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopecia, with a refractory perineal rash, is zinc deficiency: oral zinc supplementation. A yeast rash stays in the diaper area without perioral or scalp findings, and atopic dermatitis does not explain the diarrhea or the hair loss
  20. 11-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 4 days Recovered last week from 5 days of watery diarrhea beefy-red plaques in the inguinal creases satellite papules at the border Afebrile · well appearing → Fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the skin barrier → stool raises the local pH (the breakdown of urinary urea), which can increase fecal enzyme activity and further damage the skin; Candida albicans from the gut then colonizes the broken skin. Zinc depletion needs chronic diarrhea with perioral dermatitis and alopecia
  21. 10-month-old girl has had a diaper rash for 1 week beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases satellite lesions beyond the border Her parent asks which treatments are safe Afebrile · well appearing → A high-potency topical corticosteroid → high-potency steroids should not be used on the groin or under occlusion, except in rare situations and for short durations, and a diaper occludes; atrophy and striae are the risk. Nystatin under a barrier is the treatment
  22. 4-year-old girl has had vulvar itching for 3 days Toilet trained; finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week erythema over vulva and perineum into the inguinal creases satellite papules; thick white discharge at the introitus Afebrile → Candidal vulvovaginitis → redness of the vulva and perineum into the creases with satellite papules and a thick white discharge after antibiotics is yeast: a topical antifungal such as nystatin. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases, and perianal streptococcal disease is a sharply demarcated perianal rash
How NBME framed it: question 1

2-day-old girl examined before discharge home Term baby; uncomplicated pregnancy; spontaneous vaginal delivery length 50 cm · weight 3515 g · T 36.8 °C · HR 128/min · respirations 38/min · BP 70/54 mm Hg rash all over: tiny yellow papules on red skin mostly on the trunk

Most appropriate next step?

Competing answers
  • Lesion culture and antibiotics against Staphylococcus aureus: pustules suggest a bacterial infection; but impetigo is a superficial erosion with a honey-colored crust, and localized disease takes topical mupirocin.
  • Herpes simplex virus culture of a lesion: any newborn rash raises herpes; but herpes gives grouped vesicles, and these are papules on a red base in a well baby.
  • Potassium hydroxide prep of a scraping for Candida: papules on a red base could be yeast; but yeast sits in the diaper area as beefy-red plaques with satellite pustules, and this rash is on the trunk.
  • Topical corticosteroid: the skin is inflamed; but a self-limited rash needs no steroid.

Down to two: reassurance or a herpes culture. Reassurance: small yellow papules on a red base, mostly over the trunk, in a well 2-day-old are erythema toxicum, a clinical diagnosis that clears without treatment; a smear, if done, shows eosinophils. Each decoy fits another rash.

How NBME framed it: question 2

5-year-old girl with 5 days of worsening dysuria and vaginal redness Her mother saw a little yellow discharge in her underwear No fever, vomiting or diarrhea; healthy, on no medications No history of sexual abuse vital signs normal moderate erythema over the vagina and whole perineum, perianal skin included no vesicles or pustules; scant white discharge at the introitus Rest of the exam normal; culture of the discharge pending

Most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

Competing answers
  • Intramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin: a genital rash with discharge raises a sexually transmitted infection; but gonorrhea and chlamydia give mucopurulent discharge, not white, and in a prepubertal child past the newborn period either would also prompt a sexual abuse evaluation.
  • Oral acyclovir: genital pain and redness; but herpes simplex virus gives painful vesicles on a red base, and there are none.
  • Oral amoxicillin: burning with urination suggests cystitis; but redness over the vulva and perineum with white discharge points to yeast.
  • Oral metronidazole: a vaginal discharge; but its spectrum is obligate anaerobic bacteria and protozoa such as Trichomonas vaginalis (it is the antibiotic of choice for bacterial vaginosis), and this is yeast; topical agents are preferred for superficial candidiasis.

Down to two: topical nystatin or oral amoxicillin. Topical nystatin: candidal vulvovaginitis in a girl past the diaper years. The stem opens on burning with urination and closes on a pending culture, while the diagnosis sits in the white discharge and the perineal-to-perianal redness. Risk factors include diabetes mellitus, recent antibiotics and corticosteroids; none is required.

Management
By rash Erythema toxicum – reassurance: educate the parents about its benign course; it fades over 5 to 7 days and may recur for several weeks; no treatment is needed · Transient neonatal pustular melanosis – observe; no treatment is necessary · Milia – observe; reassurance about the benign, self-limited course; do not extract · Miliaria rubra – a cool environment, no overbundling, loose, thin, breathable cotton; a mild- to mid-potency topical steroid may be applied if severe · Cephalic pustulosis – observe (weeks to months); if the look bothers the parents, a topical antifungal such as ketoconazole can be used safely and may help · Seborrheic dermatitis – reassurance and watchful waiting; an emollient and gentle brushing with a soft brush can loosen the scale; topical ketoconazole is safe in infants · Irritant diaper dermatitis – a barrier such as zinc oxide or petrolatum, and frequent diaper changes; a short course of a low-potency steroid can be used if not improving within 2 to 3 days, or in moderate to severe cases · Candidal diaper dermatitis – topical nystatin with every diaper change, applied under the barrier ointment; switch to an azole (clotrimazole, miconazole or ketoconazole, twice daily for 7 to 10 days) if no improvement by 1 to 3 days; add oral nystatin for thrush; avoid a high-potency steroid under a diaper, which occludes
Not benign: red flags and the dangerous mimics Red flags: palms or soles involved in an otherwise erythema toxicum picture, vesicles or crusting, or fever or irritability; any one means the rash is not benign. Pustular melanosis, present at birth and nonerythematous, is the benign rash that may reach the palms and soles. Neonatal HSV: clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5 to 14; PCR and IV acyclovir. Congenital syphilis: maculopapular rash that includes the palms and soles, snuffles, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, no pustules; IV penicillin. Staphylococcal pustulosis: localized pustules, vesicles or bullae that rupture to honey-colored crusts, in the diaper area or at a wound such as a circumcision; topical mupirocin. Blueberry muffin rash: TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus). Langerhans cell histiocytosis: looks seborrheic but is petechial and does not resolve. Maternal cold sores: do not diagnose HSV in a well 2-day-old with erythematous pustules and spared palms and soles; base the diagnosis on the morphology and the infant's well appearance.
Worse after it got better The diagnosis rests on the trajectory, not the morphology. A barrier is the correct and sufficient treatment for irritant dermatitis, so a rash that improved on it and then worsened has a superinfection, not a new diagnosis; a rash failing first-line therapy from the start would instead question the original diagnosis. Two examination findings name the cause: the rash involves the skinfolds, and it has satellite lesions, discrete red papules beyond the border of the main plaque, the most characteristic and near-specific feature of Candida. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases because the convex surfaces touch the wet diaper and the depths of the folds are protected; Candida thrives in the warm, occluded crease. Recent diarrhea is the risk factor, not a diagnosis: a higher local pH can increase fecal enzyme activity and damage the barrier, and Candida albicans from the gut then colonizes the skin. Expect it after recent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, or with oral thrush. The antifungal goes under the barrier, not instead of it, because the skin is still broken and still in contact with stool.
Reading the stem Run the spine: did first-line therapy work and then stop? Folds involved? Satellites? Does the rash leave the diaper area (scabies)? Is the diarrhea chronic, with perioral rash and alopecia (zinc)? Is any lesion itself a sexually transmitted infection? If none is, nothing licenses an abuse workup. Afebrile, eating and sleeping normally means not systemically ill; fussiness only during changes is local pain. Social details such as separated parents or day care raise abuse and contagion, but neither is an examination finding, and no affected classmate excludes contagion. The initial improvement on the barrier is the single most informative detail.
Other newborn skin findings Congenital dermal melanocytosis: blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, benign and self-resolving by age 3 to 5 years; document them on exam to avoid confusion with non-accidental trauma. Acrocyanosis (symmetric blue-purple hands and feet with crying or cold), cutis marmorata (symmetric lacy violaceous mottling of the limbs that changes with temperature) and harlequin color change (sharply demarcated redness of one side of the body) are clinical diagnoses that need no treatment.
Common wrong answers Oral amoxicillin for a refractory diaper rash: bacterial superinfection is real, but perianal streptococcal disease is bright red and sharply demarcated around the anus. Topical permethrin: scabies causes refractory diaper rash in infants, but it is diffuse across the trunk, axillae, palms and soles, with an affected contact. Oral zinc after a diarrheal illness: acrodermatitis enteropathica needs chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis and alopecia. Screening for sexual abuse: triggered by findings that are themselves sexually transmitted infections; a social detail is not a finding.
Pairs with Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle (transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited) and vaginal discharge in a newborn girl: is the discharge white with perineal redness, or mucoid in a well newborn?
Transferable rule

Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure (bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position); when the history describes the environment, removing that exposure is the treatment. When a correct treatment works and then stops working, the diagnosis was not wrong; something was added. Ask what the first treatment does not cover, and look for the finding that identifies it.

Diabetes Complications and Annual Care

the annual care bundle and the outcome noun · kidney screening by detection threshold · foot ulcers read by exam, not risk profileIs the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit, which test catches the reversible stage, and does the exam overrule the risk profile?

Annual careKidneyFootPractice
Bottom line

Read the outcome noun before the options.

  • Morbidity: disease burden (complications and disability), so preventing it in diabetes means screening for a complication.
  • Mortality: death.
  • Dilated eye exam: finds retinopathy, the most common preventable complication; asymptomatic until advanced, and the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.
  • Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (UACR): the kidney screen, because the most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold. It detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible window; the dipstick turns positive only at about 300 mg/day or more and depends on urine concentration.
  • Persistent albuminuria: with hypertension, if not pregnant, an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB); in type 2 diabetes with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 20 mL/min/1.73 m² or more, add a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor; never an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.
  • Hyperfiltration: early nephropathy can keep creatinine normal or low while glomeruli are lost, so a normal creatinine does not exclude early diabetic kidney disease.
  • Neuropathic ulcer: painless, plantar over a bony prominence, on a warm foot. Together these point away from arterial disease, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so pulses and an ankle-brachial index (ABI) are still checked: a normal ABI, with a normal toe-brachial index, makes arterial disease less likely but cannot exclude it, since calcified vessels raise the ABI. Warm means perfused; dry means autonomic denervation. Diabetes is the most common cause.
  • Three tests, three questions: a culture characterizes the wound, the ABI the perfusion; only the hemoglobin A1c identifies the underlying disease.
Annual care
The annual bundle Dilated eye exam – yearly, or every 1 to 2 years may be considered after normal exams with well-controlled glycemia; first exam at diagnosis in type 2, within 5 years of onset in adult type 1; macular edema, moderate or worse nonproliferative, or any proliferative retinopathy to ophthalmology · Monofilament foot exam – yearly; lost protective sensation means neuropathy: foot care education, podiatry, inspect the feet each visit · UACR with serum creatinine – yearly · Blood pressure – every visit · Lipids – at least every 5 years · Counseling – depression screening; weight and tobacco counseling · A1c – every 3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; every 6 months when stable at goal · Pneumococcal vaccine – diabetes is a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49; every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
Outcome word → intervention selected
The stem asksIt meansIt selects
Prevent morbidityComplications, disabilityScreening for the complication
Reduce mortalityDeathInterventions with survival data (long-term oxygen in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)
Reduce hospitalizationAdmissionsThe driver of decompensation (blood pressure control in heart failure)
Most beneficialMagnitude, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
Kidney

Other question verbs Quantify total protein – when a non-albumin protein is suspected: urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour protein; dipstick and UACR miss light chains (myeloma: dipstick negative, sulfosalicylic acid test positive, urine protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike) · Most accurate glomerular filtration rate (GFR) – measured clearance (inulin or iothalamate); cystatin C when creatinine is unreliable (amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders, cirrhosis)

Foot
Leg and foot ulcer types

ABI bands (American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association) and neuropathy ABI over 1.4 – noncompressible, calcified vessels (diabetes, end-stage renal disease): use the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less · 1.0 to 1.4 – normal · 0.91 to 0.99 – borderline · 0.90 or less – abnormal · 0.5 to 0.9 – claudication · Under 0.4 – critical limb ischemia · Small-fiber neuropathy – pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction · Large-fiber neuropathy – sensory loss, which lets injury go unrecognized · Timing – peripheral neuropathy can be present when type 2 diabetes is diagnosed
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman had type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago Asymptomatic; walks daily and has cut out sugary drinks takes metformin; no other medical history BP 122/78 mm Hg · A1c 6.1% → Annual dilated eye exam → morbidity means the complications of diabetes, so the answer screens for one: the dilated eye exam finds retinopathy while it is still asymptomatic. Pneumococcal vaccination is indicated too, but it addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes; monthly A1c measures overlapping windows
  2. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 6 years Due for his annual kidney screening; feels well takes metformin; no edema BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · A1c 7.4% → Spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio → the most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold: the ratio detects 30 to 300 mg/g, the reversible stage. The dipstick stays negative until about 300 mg/day; a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour collection quantifies total protein when a non-albumin protein is suspected
  3. 45-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had a foot ulcer for 3 weeks painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head surrounding callus; foot warm and dry T 36.9 °C · pedal pulses normal · A1c 9.1% → Neuropathic ulcer → painless, plantar over a bony prominence and warm point away from arterial disease; normal pulses support a perfused foot, but neuropathy hides ischemic pain, so the ABI is still checked, and even a normal ABI and toe-brachial index only make arterial disease less likely; dry skin is autonomic denervation. Off-loading with a total contact cast is the single most important treatment, with debridement and glycemic control
  4. 56-year-old man has type 2 diabetes diagnosed today Thirst and frequent urination for 2 months no medical care in the past 10 years BP 134/84 mm Hg · A1c 8.2% · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → At diagnosis → in type 2 diabetes kidney screening starts at diagnosis and repeats yearly, because silent hyperglycemia predates the diagnosis by years; in type 1 it starts 5 years after diagnosis
  5. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 2 years asks about A1c frequency A1c at goal on her last three checks No change in her metformin dose for a year BP 118/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.4% → Check the A1c every 6 months → stable at goal means every 6 months; every 3 months is for an A1c not at goal or after a therapy change. Monthly values measure overlapping windows of the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan
  6. 68-year-old man has had a painful ulcer at the toe tips for 1 month pain worse with the leg raised, better dangling cool pale foot; shiny, hairless skin T 36.8 °C · BP 148/86 mm Hg · absent pulses → Arterial ischemic ulcer → a painful ulcer at the toe tips on a cool, pale, pulseless foot is arterial: confirm with the ankle-brachial index. A neuropathic ulcer is painless and plantar on a warm foot; a venous ulcer is wet and sits at the medial malleolus
  7. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a single abnormal albumin-to-creatinine ratio ratio 64 mg/g on his annual screen Ran a 10K race the day before the sample BP 126/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Repeat the albumin-to-creatinine ratio → confirmation requires 2 of 3 abnormal samples over 3 to 6 months, which excludes transient albuminuria from exercise, fever, infection, heart failure or hyperglycemia; drug treatment starts once it persists
  8. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is due for vaccines Receives this season's influenza vaccine today no asplenia; no chronic lung or heart disease Does not smoke BP 120/76 mm Hg · A1c 6.8% → Pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is a risk-based indication for pneumococcal vaccination in adults 19 to 49, and every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age; asplenia is not required
  9. 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years is seen for his annual foot exam ABI 1.5 in both legs radiograph shows calcified tibial arteries BP 138/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Noncompressible vessels → an index over 1.4 means calcified, noncompressible vessels, as in diabetes and end-stage renal disease; the next test is the toe-brachial index, abnormal at 0.7 or less, which can unmask arterial disease the ABI hides
  10. 24-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 Establishing care at a new clinic after a move uses an insulin pump; no kidney screening on record BP 112/70 mm Hg · A1c 7.3% → 5 Years after diagnosis → in type 1 diabetes kidney screening starts 5 years after diagnosis, then yearly; it starts at diagnosis only in type 2, where hyperglycemia has been silent for years
  11. 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes asks what most reduces his risk of death smokes one pack of cigarettes daily Overdue for his eye and foot exams BP 136/84 mm Hg · A1c 7.0% → Smoking cessation → mortality means death, so choose the intervention with survival data: smoking cessation, then blood pressure control and a statin. The eye and foot exams prevent morbidity, not death
  12. 62-year-old woman has had a leg ulcer for 2 months shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus brown hemosiderin staining and ankle edema Mild ache, better with the leg raised T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Venous stasis ulcer → a shallow, wet ulcer at the medial malleolus with hemosiderin and edema is venous stasis: duplex ultrasound, then compression
  13. 60-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 9 years albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g second elevated value in 4 months; the first was 72 mg/g BP 134/82 mm Hg (similar at her last visit) · A1c 7.1% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor → persistent albuminuria (2 of 3 samples elevated over 3 to 6 months) with a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg calls for an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more an SGLT2 inhibitor as well; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts her eGFR well above 20. Together they are most likely to slow progression
  14. 61-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer that has not healed in 2 months plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence; probe-to-bone test positive Foot radiograph normal T 37.2 °C · ESR 88 mm/h → Osteomyelitis → a probe that touches bone makes osteomyelitis likely, and an ESR over 70 supports it; plain films are insensitive early, so MRI comes next, then bone biopsy, which names the organism
  15. 28-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes asks when to recheck her A1c A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent Takes metformin and sitagliptin; no low blood sugars BP 124/78 mm Hg · weight 82 kg → Check the A1c every 3 months → an A1c not at goal and a therapy change each mean every 3 months; every 6 months is for an A1c stable at goal
  16. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is enrolling in a drug study below-knee amputation of the right leg last year The study protocol needs an exact filtration rate before dosing BP 130/80 mm Hg · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Inulin or iothalamate clearance → measured clearance is the most accurate; creatinine is unreliable in amputees, cachexia, bodybuilders and cirrhosis, where cystatin C helps
  17. 58-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has a warm, swollen, erythematous right foot swelling for 3 weeks no ulcer or break in the skin; no fever Cannot feel the monofilament on either foot T 36.9 °C · white cells 7,400/mm³ → Charcot arthropathy → a warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests Charcot arthropathy (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
  18. 32-year-old woman has type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 26 Establishing care after a move; old records lost reports she has never had a dilated eye examination BP 116/72 mm Hg · A1c 7.6% → Within 5 years after diagnosis → in an adult with type 1 diabetes the first dilated eye exam comes within 5 years after onset, then yearly; in type 2 diabetes it comes at diagnosis. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced, so waiting for symptoms misses it
  19. 34-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging painful ulcer on her lower leg violaceous, undermined border grew from a small sore over 10 days Has inflammatory bowel disease with a recent flare T 37.3 °C · white cells 9,800/mm³ → Pyoderma gangrenosum → a rapidly enlarging, very painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis is pyoderma gangrenosum: biopsy and steroids, and never debride (pathergy)
  20. 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has confirmed albuminuria ratio 140 mg/g, then 156 mg/g 3 months later Asks what most slows progression BP 138/86 mm Hg (similar at his last visit) · A1c 7.8% · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → ACE inhibitor or ARB plus an SGLT2 inhibitor → with albuminuria and a blood pressure above the American Diabetes Association target of under 130/80 mm Hg, an ACE inhibitor or ARB plus, in type 2 diabetes with an eGFR of 20 or more, an SGLT2 inhibitor slows progression; a creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL puts his eGFR well above 20. Never combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB
  21. 66-year-old man has a chronic non-healing ulcer on his shin arose in an old burn scar 8 months ago rolled, everted edges No better despite compression and two courses of antibiotics T 36.8 °C · pedal pulses normal → Biopsy for Marjolin ulcer → an ulcer in a chronic wound or scar with rolled, everted edges that has not healed in over 3 months needs a biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
Management Neuropathic ulcer – off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention; debride callus and necrotic tissue; glycemic control · Infection – culture only if clinically infected, deep tissue rather than a swab · Perfusion – check the ABI anyway: mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common · Charcot arthropathy – warm, swollen, red foot with no ulcer, fever or raised white count in a diabetic with peripheral neuropathy suggests it (confirm with radiographs or MRI): immobilize; rocker-bottom deformity
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90 to 120 day red cell lifespan, so monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows; they add no information and prevent no complication. At goal, monthly testing is six times the 6-month schedule.
⚠︎ Two problems with the source explanation The source question for the first practice item (eye exam, pneumococcal vaccine or monthly A1c to prevent morbidity) came with two errors. 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It limited vaccination to patients over 65 or with asplenia, but every adult 50 or older is vaccinated by age, and diabetes is itself a risk-based indication in adults 19 to 49, so she is a candidate. The eye exam wins because it targets a diabetes-specific complication; vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes. 2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals come from the American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care, not the USPSTF.
Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing “Microalbuminuria” → “UACR 85 mg/g” · “hyperfiltration” → “creatinine 0.7” in a diabetic · “Kimmelstiel-Wilson” → “nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy” · “transient albuminuria” → “he ran a 10K yesterday.”
Transferable rule

Read the outcome noun before the options: morbidity, mortality, hospitalization and benefit are four different targets, and a distractor can be the right intervention for the wrong target. The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold; the most specific or confirmatory test is the least likely to give a false positive. Risk factors set the prior probability and physical findings the posterior: when the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, rely on the exam.

Vaccines in Pregnancy

choosing the vaccine or immunoglobulin due now · the Tdap window optimizes protection; it is not an eligibility gateWhich one is due now, and is this window a gate or an optimization?

What is dueAnti-DVaricellaPractice
Bottom line

The patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins; give the one that is due now. A date, a gestational age or a serology decides which one is due, not a symptom.

  • Tdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis): every pregnancy, irrespective of prior Tdap; optimal at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably the earlier part, although Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy.
  • The window is an optimization, not a gate: for a wound needing tetanus prophylaxis or a community pertussis outbreak, give Tdap then; a dose given earlier in pregnancy is not repeated at 27 to 36 weeks.
  • Inactivated influenza vaccine: any trimester while flu viruses circulate; in the first or second trimester, preferably September or October; in the third trimester, July or August can be considered. The classic visit is in mid-September, so it is due.
  • Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine: one dose of RSV prefusion F (RSVpreF; Abrysvo, the only one for pregnancy) at 32 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks, September through January in most of the United States; or infant nirsevimab. Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy; after a prior-pregnancy dose, the infant gets nirsevimab instead.
  • Measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) and varicella vaccines: live, contraindicated in pregnancy; if not immune, give after pregnancy, before discharge (varicella: a second dose 4 to 8 weeks later if never vaccinated).
  • Hepatitis B vaccine: if not already vaccinated, vaccinate in pregnancy (not PreHevbrio, which lacks pregnancy safety data).
  • Anti-D immunoglobulin: routinely at 28 weeks when Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen.
What is due now

The classic patient: Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen, non-immune to rubella, varicella immunoglobulin G (IgG) positive after a recent exposure, seen in mid-September.

Option analysis: why each fails
ChoiceWhy it temptsWhat kills it
Anti-D immunoglobulinShe is Rh-negative with a negative screenTiming: routine prophylaxis at 28 weeks
MMRShe is non-immune to rubellaLive, contraindicated; give after pregnancy, before discharge
TdapIndicated in every pregnancyTiming, as an optimization, not a gate: 27 to 36 weeks maximizes transplacental IgG transfer
Varicella vaccineRecent exposureLive, contraindicated, and she is already immune
Varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG)Exposure plus pregnancy is the classic postexposure prophylaxis settingVaricella IgG positive = immune; prophylaxis is for the non-immune

Two fail on timing, two on live-vaccine status, one on serology. Each distractor fails for a different reason: eliminate each on its own terms rather than comparing them.

Vaccines in pregnancy
RecommendedIf indicated or at riskNot in pregnancy
Inactivated influenza, seasonal; Tdap every pregnancy; RSV vaccine at 32 to 36 weeks, September to January; hepatitis B if not already vaccinated (not PreHevbrio); anti-D at 28 weeks if Rh-negative with a negative antibody screenHepatitis A if at risk for infection or a severe outcome; meningococcal vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y if indicated; VZIG if exposed and non-immuneMMR, varicella, live attenuated influenza (LAIV), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guerin), oral polio: live vaccines are generally contraindicated. Human papillomavirus (HPV): not live, but deferred until after pregnancy. Recombinant zoster: no recommendation; consider delaying

No recommendation: pneumococcal vaccines (limited safety data) and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b). Newborns of mothers given the pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine by mistake in pregnancy do not seem to be at increased risk.

COVID-19 ⚠︎: the CDC pregnancy table today gives no guidance, while the CDC 2026-2027 guidance recommends a COVID-19 vaccine for all adults 18 years and older, and the CDC pregnancy page (February 2026) says the 2025-2026 recommendations are based on individual decision making; check the current schedule.

Anti-D immunoglobulin
Rh immunoglobulin timing 28 weeks routinely; within 72 hours of delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive; any sensitizing event: vaginal bleeding, spontaneous or threatened abortion, ectopic or molar pregnancy, amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, external cephalic version, abdominal trauma. A positive anti-D screen with no recent anti-D immunoglobulin means she is already alloimmunized, so anti-D can no longer help: switch to titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler.
Varicella in pregnancy
Varicella in pregnancy Non-immune and exposed: VZIG as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Maternal varicella can cause varicella pneumonia (high mortality): intravenous acyclovir. Congenital varicella syndrome at 8 to 20 weeks (first or early second trimester; small risk, 0.4 to 2.0%): limb hypoplasia, cicatricial dermatomal scarring, chorioretinitis, cataracts. Neonatal varicella if the maternal rash occurs 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: VZIG to the newborn.
Practice
  1. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation asks which vaccines she needs First pregnancy; healthy, no medications Last Tdap at age 12 fetal heart tones present BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap at 27 to 36 weeks → Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, and the antibody transfer that protects the newborn is maximized at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably early in that window: schedule it; do not decline it. Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy, but a dose given earlier is not repeated in the window. Postpartum Tdap gives the infant no immunity. Give influenza vaccine now if it is in season
  2. 28-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation was exposed to chickenpox 3 days ago Her nephew's vesicular rash began the next day No history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination no rash Afebrile · varicella IgG negative → VZIG as soon as possible → a negative varicella IgG means she is not immune, so varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) is due: as soon as possible, within 10 days of exposure. Varicella vaccine is live and contraindicated in pregnancy. Acyclovir treats varicella once the rash appears; it is not the prophylaxis here
  3. 26-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit in October She has had no influenza vaccine this season Healthy; takes only a prenatal vitamin Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Inactivated influenza vaccine today → no gestational window: inactivated influenza vaccine can be given at any time during pregnancy in the season, preferably September or October in the first or second trimester; the live attenuated vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy
  4. 23-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation has had light vaginal bleeding since this morning Blood type A, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative closed cervix; fetal heart tones present HR 82/min · BP 114/70 mm Hg → Anti-D now, regardless of gestational age → vaginal bleeding is a sensitizing event, so anti-D is given now, regardless of gestational age; it is not held for the routine 28-week dose
  5. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation reviews her first prenatal labs Rubella IgG negative; varicella IgG positive asks whether she can be vaccinated against rubella now Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg → MMR postpartum before discharge → non-immune rubella is a classic stem: MMR is live and contraindicated in pregnancy, so give it after pregnancy, before discharge. It is not contraindicated for life
  6. 26-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation stepped on a rusty nail in her garden dirty puncture wound of the sole Last tetanus and diphtheria (Td) booster 12 years ago Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg → Tdap now → a tetanus-containing vaccine is indicated for this wound, and in a pregnant woman that dose is Tdap, given now: the window does not apply to prophylaxis. A dose given earlier in pregnancy is not repeated at 27 to 36 weeks
  7. 27-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has 4 days of a vesicular rash and 1 day of cough and dyspnea Her son had chickenpox 2 weeks ago T 38.4 °C · respiratory rate 28/min · oxygen saturation 91% on room air → Varicella pneumonia → a varicella rash with dyspnea in pregnancy is varicella pneumonia, with high mortality: treat with intravenous acyclovir. Disseminated herpes zoster is a reactivation of latent infection, not a first infection after a chickenpox contact
  8. 26-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation in her first pregnancy comes for a visit in November She has not received a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine healthy Afebrile · BP 114/72 mm Hg → RSVpreF now → one dose of Abrysvo at 32 0/7 through 36 6/7 weeks, September through January, protects the newborn; otherwise plan nirsevimab for the infant. Most infants will not need both. Unlike Tdap, CDC does not currently recommend repeating it in a later pregnancy. The vaccine is recommended in pregnancy, not contraindicated
  9. 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Blood type B, Rh-negative No anti-D immunoglobulin this pregnancy antibody screen positive for anti-D BP 110/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 148/min → Antibody titers with serial MCA Dopplers → with no anti-D immunoglobulin given, a positive anti-D screen means she is already alloimmunized, and anti-D cannot undo it; follow titers and middle cerebral artery (MCA) Doppler. The repeat screen at 24 to 28 weeks is for unsensitized women
  10. 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation in her second pregnancy Received Tdap at 29 weeks in her first pregnancy 2 years ago asks whether she needs it again BP 116/74 mm Hg · Afebrile → Give Tdap again → Tdap is given during each pregnancy, irrespective of a prior dose, because it protects this infant. Td lacks the pertussis component
  11. 21-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation asks about her human papillomavirus vaccine She received the first dose of a 3-dose series 2 months ago first prenatal visit BP 108/66 mm Hg · Afebrile → Defer to postpartum → HPV vaccines are not recommended in pregnancy; the rest of the series is delayed until the pregnancy is complete. The vaccine is not live and is not contraindicated for life; a dose given by mistake in pregnancy needs no intervention
  12. 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit Blood type O, Rh-negative; antibody screen negative Received Tdap at 27 weeks and influenza vaccine in October BP 116/72 mm Hg · fundal height 28 cm → Anti-D immunoglobulin → she is Rh-negative with a negative screen, and routine prophylaxis is due at 28 weeks. Tdap given earlier in this pregnancy is not repeated, and this season's influenza dose is done
  13. 26-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation is offered the nasal influenza vaccine at a pharmacy in October No influenza vaccine this season healthy; no egg allergy Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine → the nasal formulation is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give the intramuscular inactivated vaccine, in any trimester during the season. Influenza vaccine is right; that influenza vaccine is wrong
  14. 26-year-old woman received MMR vaccine 3 weeks ago, then discovered she is pregnant Last menstrual period 7 weeks ago she asks whether the pregnancy is at risk Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg → Counsel and reassure; not an indication for termination → MMR inadvertently given in pregnancy: counsel her about the theoretical risk to the fetus; MMR vaccination during pregnancy is not a reason to terminate. The guidance calls for counseling about the theoretical risk, not fetal surveillance
  15. 25-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation comes for a prenatal visit Rh-negative; received anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks Rubella IgG negative; no Tdap yet this pregnancy BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap → Tdap is due in every pregnancy, optimally at 27 to 36 weeks, preferably early in that window, so 30 weeks is the time. Anti-D was given at 28 weeks. MMR is live and contraindicated in pregnancy; give it after pregnancy, before discharge
  16. 31-year-old woman delivered a healthy term girl 1 day ago A vesicular rash appeared on her face and trunk 3 days before delivery No history of chickenpox mother T 37.8 °C · newborn HR 142/min → VZIG to the neonate → a maternal varicella rash from 5 days before to 2 days after delivery puts the newborn at risk: give varicella zoster immune globulin (VZIG) to the newborn. The live varicella vaccine is not the newborn's prophylaxis
  17. 34-year-old man asks about vaccines; his partner is at 32 weeks' gestation He has never received Tdap His mother, who will help care for the newborn, has not received it either Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Vaccinate them at least 2 weeks before contact → people who are not up to date should get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant (cocooning)
  18. 32-year-old woman is breastfeeding on the day after a vaginal delivery Rubella IgG negative on prenatal labs Received Tdap at 28 weeks; completed the HPV vaccine series at age 12 Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg → MMR → MMR after pregnancy, before discharge, for a patient without rubella immunity; it is safe while breastfeeding. Tdap is given immediately postpartum only when it was not given during pregnancy and she has never had Tdap, and her HPV series is complete
  19. 26-year-old woman is breastfeeding her 6-week-old son Rubella IgG and varicella IgG negative on prenatal labs asks whether vaccines are safe for her baby while she is nursing Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg → Inactivated and live vaccines are both permitted → neither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety, so MMR and varicella vaccine can be given now: the restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation. The exceptions are smallpox vaccine (contraindicated) and yellow fever vaccine (avoided unless travel cannot be postponed)
Why maternal Tdap Maternal Tdap is for the infant: the childhood pertussis series does not start until 2 months, and most infant pertussis deaths occur before that protection. It takes about 2 weeks after Tdap for the mother to be protected, and the antibody then needs time to cross, so late-third-trimester dosing is suboptimal; preterm delivery is the reason to dose at 27 weeks, not 36. Postpartum Tdap gives the infant no immunity. Household contacts who are not up to date get Tdap at least 2 weeks before meeting the infant.
Breastfeeding The vaccine restrictions apply to pregnancy, not lactation: neither inactivated nor live vaccines given to a lactating woman affect breastfeeding safety. Exceptions: smallpox vaccine is contraindicated and yellow fever vaccine is avoided unless travel cannot be postponed.
Common wrong answers Class versus member: influenza vaccine is right, but the live attenuated nasal one is wrong in pregnancy. Sequencing: Tdap today at 10 weeks, or deferred to postpartum, instead of scheduled at 27 to 36 weeks. Skipping Tdap because she had it last pregnancy: it is for this fetus.
Transferable rule

When a patient will eventually need several vaccines or immunoglobulins, check the number (date, gestational age or titer) before weighing the indications. When a recommendation carries a time window, ask what it protects: if it optimizes an effect (antibody transfer), move outside it when the indication changes; if it defines eligibility (age 21 for cytology), you cannot.
