Brain Tumors in a Child

sellar and suprasellar masses that announce themselves on the growth chart, and posterior fossa masses that announce themselves on the neurologic examinationIs the abnormal finding endocrine or neurologic; for the sella, does the axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and for the posterior fossa, which side and which structure?

DiagnosisPracticeWorkup and management
Bottom line

Ask where the abnormal finding sits. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty with a normal neurologic examination points to the sella; ataxia or crossed findings point to the posterior fossa, where you localize side first and structure second. Image with MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); with papilledema, never tap first.

  • Suprasellar mass: classically a normal neurologic examination (no dysmetria, gait abnormality, focal weakness or skin findings); height crosses downward through percentiles while weight holds, with Tanner 1 past the pubertal gate and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one; arrested puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed, and multiple axes point to the stalk, not the gland. Headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus make the mass midline and suprasellar.
  • Craniopharyngioma: from Rathke pouch remnants; cystic and calcified suprasellar mass on MRI; subtle for years before diagnosis.
  • Posterior fossa mass: 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumors but only 15 to 20% of adult ones, so in a child, ataxia with raised pressure is infratentorial until imaged. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral.
  • Hemisphere or vermis: limb dysmetria is hemispheric; a midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared. Both together mean a hemispheric mass large enough to disturb midline structures; ipsilateral facial numbness fits (the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally), and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression.
  • Crossed findings: a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long-tract weakness on the other mean brainstem.
Diagnosis
Localizing signs Cerebellar signs – ipsilateral; the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion; face also ipsilateral; body long tracts contralateral · Hemisphere – limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline – truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus – direction-changing, gaze-evoked and unsuppressed; peripheral (vertigo) nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation · Raised-pressure headache – daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema · Growth failure – downward crossing of height percentiles after a stable channel, weight preserved; endocrine causes such as growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism keep a normal or increased weight, and in poor nutrition weight loss comes before height loss · Pubertal delay – no breast development by age 13 in girls; Tanner 1 at 13 meets it · Stalk pattern – multiple anterior axes down, with or without posterior failure (diabetes insipidus); stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly growth failure from TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) or growth hormone deficiency; morning cortisol, free T4 (thyroxine), TSH and IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1) come back low in more than one axis · Gland pattern – a single hypersecreting axis with the others intact
Where is the mass
LocationTumorTell
Suprasellar, midlineCraniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; the adamantinomatous type peaks at 5 to 14 and 50 to 74 yearsCystic and calcified; growth failure, pubertal delay, bitemporal hemianopsia; years of subtle symptoms
Suprasellar or pineal, midlineGerminoma (can't miss): germ cell tumor; adolescent, often maleDiabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes; beta-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) usually negative in a pure germinoma, though low beta-hCG can be detected; radiosensitive
IntrasellarProlactinoma or other pituitary adenoma; adolescent or adultNon-calcified; one axis hypersecreting, others intact; galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic features
Optic chiasm or nerveOptic pathway glioma (pilocytic astrocytoma); young child, often NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1)Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with a normal appetite)
SellaRathke cleft cyst: same embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headache
Pituitary stalkLangerhans cell histiocytosis; young childCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk; lytic skull lesions; seborrheic scalp rash
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classicallyCyst with a mural nodule; ipsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia; falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma; early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, limbs relatively spared; typically hyperdense on CT (computed tomography), with restricted diffusion; seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid)
Fourth ventricleEpendymomaTends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle; calcification and cysts common
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia still ipsilateral: a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
PonsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings: cranial nerve palsy one side (diplopia from an abducens palsy is often first), long-tract weakness the other; diffuse pontine expansion
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome: upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia
Occipital lobeSupratentorial massContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Practice
  1. 14-year-old girl, a year of headaches, now worse height fell from 40th to 3rd percentile over 2 years weight steady at 70th percentile; Tanner 1 Skin, neurologic examination normal; no focal deficit Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · optic disc edema → Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass → height falling while weight holds is endocrine, and Tanner 1 at 14 is a second failed axis, so the stalk is involved; with headache and disc edema the mass is midline and suprasellar, cystic and calcified: craniopharyngioma. A vermian tumor brings truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared, and this examination is clean; subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis, a skin-first diagnosis that does not arrest linear growth
  2. 9-year-old boy, 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia gait lists to the left left facial numbness No weakness or sensory loss in the limbs BP 118/72 mm Hg · bilateral papilledema → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → every cerebellar sign is on the left, and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the output decussates twice; limb dysmetria is hemispheric, the face is served ipsilaterally, and papilledema comes from fourth-ventricular compression. The right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side, and a frontal lobe mass gives contralateral weakness
  3. 12-year-old girl, 6 months of morning headaches height crossed from the 75th to the 10th percentile weight steady at the 60th percentile Tanner 1; neurologic examination otherwise normal T 36.8 °C · BP 108/66 mm Hg · papilledema → MRI of the brain with contrast → a height percentile crossing with weight held and papilledema is a suprasellar mass until imaged: MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar views. A bone age is nonspecific and delays the MRI when papilledema is present
  4. 6-year-old boy, 4 weeks of morning vomiting and unsteadiness truncal and gait ataxia; wide-based stance minimal limb dysmetria MRI: midline vermian mass filling the fourth ventricle, restricted diffusion, no extension through the fourth-ventricular foramina Afebrile · papilledema → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and relatively spared limbs localizes to the vermis; a midline fourth-ventricular mass with restricted diffusion in a child fits medulloblastoma, which seeds drop metastases through the CSF. A cerebellar hemisphere pilocytic astrocytoma gives ipsilateral limb signs and is classically a cyst with a mural nodule; ependymoma tends to extend through the foramen of Luschka into the cerebellopontine angle, with calcification and cysts common
  5. 9-year-old boy is seen before planned surgery MRI shows a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass Resection is planned for next week Height has slowed over 2 years; no medications BP 100/64 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → stalk compression can leave several axes deficient, so measure morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery; secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism are treated before the operation, glucocorticoid first. Growth hormone does not come before the axes that threaten the operation, and a planned resection is not a reason to wait 6 months for another MRI
  6. 5-year-old girl, 4 weeks of worsening double vision progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies right hemiparesis with brisk reflexes MRI: diffuse expansion of the pons Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → a cranial nerve palsy on one side with long-tract weakness on the other is a crossed finding, which localizes to the brainstem; diffuse expansion of the pons in a child is a diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma, and diplopia from an abducens palsy is often its first sign. Medulloblastoma and a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma give ataxia rather than crossed findings
  7. 14-year-old boy, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia urine osmolality 90 mOsm/kg non-calcified suprasellar mass CSF beta-hCG mildly elevated; serum AFP normal Growth and puberty normal so far; no rash or bone pain T 36.9 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Suprasellar germinoma → diabetes insipidus first, before the anterior axes, with a mildly raised CSF beta-hCG and a normal AFP is a suprasellar germinoma (pure germinomas usually have negative markers, but low levels of beta-hCG can be detected), which is highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy, alone or after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Craniopharyngioma is cystic and calcified, and growth hormone and gonadotropin deficits are often its first endocrine failures; Langerhans cell histiocytosis thickens the stalk and brings lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rash
  8. 9-year-old boy, 2 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting wide-based gait; right-hand dysmetria bilateral papilledema A lumbar puncture is proposed to measure the pressure T 37.0 °C · BP 116/70 mm Hg → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → papilledema with cerebellar signs means a posterior fossa mass until imaged, and lumbar puncture risks herniation, so image first: MRI of the brain instead. Measuring an opening pressure does not remove that risk, and a noncontrast CT followed by a tap still ends in the tap that papilledema with a posterior fossa mass forbids
  9. 10-year-old girl, 1 day after resection of a suprasellar tumor urine output 350 mL/h serum Na 152 mEq/L urine osmolality 85 mOsm/kg Alert and thirsty BP 104/62 mm Hg · HR 112/min → Desmopressin → dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after the stalk has been handled is central diabetes insipidus: desmopressin. Fluid restriction worsens the hypernatremia, and hypertonic saline adds sodium to a patient whose sodium is already high
  10. 12-year-old boy, 2 months of headaches and trouble looking up upgaze palsy convergence-retraction nystagmus light-near dissociation of the pupils No head trauma; visual acuity normal Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · HR 76/min → MRI of the brain, then serum and CSF tumor markers → upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation are Parinaud syndrome, a pineal-region mass; in an adolescent boy that is classically a germinoma, so obtain MRI of the brain first, then serum and CSF tumor markers, the CSF once imaging shows a tap is safe. This is not strabismus, and a noncontrast CT does not characterize the mass or the markers
  11. 8-year-old boy with a newly found suprasellar mass Vomiting and lethargic since this morning Free thyroxine low; cortisol result pending BP 84/50 mm Hg · HR 128/min · Na 128 mEq/L · glucose 52 mg/dL → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → hypotension, hyponatremia and hypoglycemia with a new suprasellar mass is adrenal crisis; give IV hydrocortisone and isotonic saline, and avoid levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement, because thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis
  12. 7-year-old boy with a right cerebellar hemisphere mass on MRI right-hand intention tremor and dysmetria falls toward the right Strength and sensation normal His parents ask why the signs are on the same side as the tumor → Cerebellar output decussates twice → cerebellar output decussates twice, so the two crossings cancel and the signs stay on the same side as the lesion. Cerebellar fibers do cross, and the cerebellum does not control the opposite limbs directly
  13. 15-year-old girl with amenorrhea and galactorrhea Normal growth; Tanner 4 MRI: 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification No headache; visual fields full BP 110/68 mm Hg · prolactin 180 ng/mL · TSH normal · urine pregnancy test negative → Prolactinoma → galactorrhea and amenorrhea with a raised prolactin, a normal TSH and pregnancy test, and a small, non-calcified intrasellar lesion with one axis hypersecreting is a prolactinoma; cabergoline is the preferred dopamine agonist. Craniopharyngioma is a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, and a Rathke cleft cyst is a non-enhancing, non-calcified cyst that is usually asymptomatic
  14. 9-year-old boy admitted with headache and vomiting MRI: posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus Over the last hour he has become drowsy Pupils equal; no seizure BP 128/70 mm Hg · HR 64/min → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and a falling level of consciousness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection. Acetazolamide with outpatient follow-up, or observation, leaves the obstruction untreated
  15. 6-year-old boy with declining vision and nystagmus several café-au-lait macules; axillary freckling thin despite a good appetite Normal stools; no bone pain or fractures Afebrile · HR 96/min · weight below the 5th percentile → MRI of the brain and orbits → café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling point to neurofibromatosis type 1, and declining vision with emaciation despite a good appetite is an optic pathway glioma with diencephalic syndrome: MRI of the brain and orbits. Celiac disease is malabsorption and brings no visual loss, and a skeletal survey looks for bone lesions he does not have
  16. 7-year-old girl with newly confirmed medulloblastoma The tumor was resected 2 weeks ago Recovering well; no back pain Leg strength and bladder function normal Neurologic examination unchanged since discharge Afebrile · no papilledema → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging is MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology, the lumbar puncture done at least 10 to 14 days after surgery. Bone marrow and whole-body imaging do not look where it spreads
  17. 11-year-old girl with a known suprasellar mass Vomiting since last night now a depressed level of consciousness CT: dilated lateral and third ventricles BP 132/60 mm Hg · HR 58/min · pupils equal → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → a suprasellar mass that blocks CSF flow at the third ventricle causes obstructive hydrocephalus; a falling level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion. Lumbar puncture risks herniation, and acetazolamide does not relieve an obstruction
  18. 4-year-old boy, 3 weeks of headache headache waking him from sleep morning vomiting Normal neurologic examination; no medications Growth chart normal; no recent head injury Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · HR 92/min → MRI of the brain → headache that wakes him from sleep, with morning vomiting, in a child under six is a red-flag headache: MRI of the brain, because a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor. A diary or migraine prophylaxis delays the diagnosis
  19. 13-year-old girl with a suprasellar mass on MRI loss of both temporal visual fields A year of headaches; height has slowed Visual acuity normal; pupils equal Her parents ask why the outer halves of her vision are missing → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → a suprasellar mass presses up on the optic chiasm, where the nasal retinal fibers, which carry the temporal fields, decussate: bitemporal hemianopsia. A lesion behind the chiasm, in the optic tract, gives a homonymous defect (the same hemifield lost in both eyes), and a Meyer loop lesion in the temporal lobe gives contralateral superior quadrantanopia
  20. 10-year-old boy treated 1 year ago with resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma Currently asymptomatic Takes hydrocortisone and levothyroxine His parents ask what follow-up he needs BP 102/64 mm Hg · height 25th percentile → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → after a craniopharyngioma, surveillance is lifelong and endocrine and visual: serial growth velocity with an annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields. Audiometry does not watch the axes or the visual fields this tumor threatens, and AFP and beta-hCG are germ cell tumor markers
Workup and management
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? If not, the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa. Plot the growth chart: height falling with weight holding is endocrine. Count failed axes: growth and puberty together are panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk. Is there posterior pituitary failure? Polyuria makes germinoma or histiocytosis more likely. Is there raised pressure or a field cut? Papilledema or bitemporal hemianopsia makes the mass midline and suprasellar, and the MRI descriptor is calcified and cystic. If the examination is focal, find the side, then the structure.
Management Before surgery – treat secondary adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism before the operation, glucocorticoid before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone increases the clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency. Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism. · After surgery – diabetes insipidus can develop in 70% after craniopharyngioma surgery; expect the sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled, and treat hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction · Obstructive hydrocephalus – a posterior fossa mass with drowsiness needs dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation, for CSF diversion then resection; a suprasellar mass with a depressed level of consciousness needs neurosurgical CSF diversion, not lumbar puncture · Germinoma – highly radiosensitive: radiation therapy alone, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by response-based radiation therapy, which has been explored to reduce radiation doses and neurodevelopmental harm · Prolactinoma – cabergoline, the preferred dopamine agonist · After craniopharyngioma – lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance, with surveillance MRI
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first.
Reading a sellar vignette Height crossing down through percentiles with weight steady is endocrine growth failure; it excludes undernutrition, which costs weight first. Tanner 1 past age 13 is gonadotropin deficiency, a second failed axis, which indicates hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. Optic disc edema without fever or neck stiffness is raised intracranial pressure without meningitis, from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle. A normal neurologic examination, including finger-nose-finger testing and gait, excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma. Normal skin excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists. No focal deficit and no fever exclude brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever. A year of headaches before worsening is a slow-growing lesion, not a reassurance; the normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise. Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging: a height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. The exception to preserved weight is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite. Diabetes insipidus first and anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma; send serum beta-hCG and AFP, and CSF levels once imaging shows a tap is safe, before assuming craniopharyngioma. Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly (height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty) but does not produce papilledema; check TSH and free T4, and disc edema separates the two. Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six. Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF, so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.
Common wrong answers Subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis and does not arrest linear growth. Tumor in the cerebellar vermis: truncal and gait ataxia with the limbs relatively spared; it does not touch the pituitary. Parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: abscess is acute, febrile and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection. Enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence. Right middle cerebellar peduncle for left-sided signs: the right region on the wrong side. Pineal mass: common in children, but it produces Parinaud syndrome. Germinoma when the anterior axes failed first and there is no polyuria; adenoma when two axes are down, there is no galactorrhea, and CSF flow is blocked; optic glioma with normal skin, normal pupils and weight preserved; Rathke cleft cyst for progressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure, too much disease for a simple cyst; histiocytosis with normal skin, no polyuria and no bone pain.
Pairs with Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in the opposite direction. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Headache in a School-Age Child: the workup before localization; is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: posterior fossa tumor as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization. Hyperprolactinemia: the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Polyuria: the step before this one; is the polyuria water or solute, and is the deprivation test still needed?
Transferable rule

When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic: a growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings, and in the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema. When the finding is neurologic, localize side first and structure second; the cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.

SSRI Adverse Effects

name the effect, then take the next stepOn the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sexual dysfunction affects more than half of patients on an SSRI and can reach desire, arousal or orgasm.

Persistent, distressing low desire: lowering the dose is the common first step, especially with the depression in sustained remission. If that fails:

  • one episode in sustained remission: consider tapering off
  • staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)

Another SSRI carries a similar risk. Sildenafil can help arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire has been shown.

FINISH symptoms typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper are discontinuation syndrome, not relapse: once other serious causes are ruled out, reassure.

Diagnosis
Which effect Sexual dysfunction – decreased desire, arousal problems or anorgasmia during SSRI therapy; increased serotonin likely explains it · Discontinuation syndrome – FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping or starting a taper (FINISH) · Serotonin syndrome – mental status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular changes, rapid onset after a medication change
FINISH
  • F – flu-like symptoms: fatigue, lethargy, malaise, muscle aches, headaches, diarrhea
  • I – insomnia
  • N – nausea
  • I – imbalance: gait instability, dizziness or lightheadedness, vertigo
  • S – sensory disturbances: paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, visual disturbance
  • H – hyperarousal: anxiety, agitation
Management and treatment
Persistent, distressing low desire on an SSRI
TierInterventionEscalate when
Common first stepLower the SSRI doseStill persistent and distressing at the lower dose
ThenOne episode, sustained remission: consider tapering off. Staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)Top rung
By situation Bulimia or seizure-prone – not bupropion (contraindicated); mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs · Arousal problems or anorgasmia – sildenafil can help; not shown to help desire · Unlikely to help or not recommended – another SSRI (similar risk; unlikely to resolve it); propranolol (unlikely to help sexual dysfunction; not helpful for depression); weekend drug holidays (not commonly used, and they interfere with the antidepressant effect)
Discontinuation syndrome
TierInterventionEscalate when
Other serious causes ruled outReassure: reversible, not serious, runs its course in 1 to 2 weeks; then consider restarting with a slow taper, or support if the patient prefers not to restartSymptoms arose during a taper
During a taperConsider restarting the original dose, then taper more slowlySlow tapering poorly tolerated
Slow taper failsConsider substituting fluoxetine for the short half-life drugTop rung
Prevention Before stopping – forewarn the patient; a supervised taper over 6 to 8 weeks may be required (another source: about 25% of the dose each week) · Choice of drug – fluoxetine, with its long half-life, is less likely than paroxetine to cause discontinuation symptoms · How long – after a first mild or moderate episode, about 6 more months after remission, then a taper over 2 months
Practice
  1. 34-year-old man, one depressive episode in remission 7 months on sertraline 150 mg daily low sexual desire since starting it it is straining his marriage no suicidal ideation · euthymic, full affect, linear thought · HR 72/min, BP 124/76 mm Hg → Lower the sertraline dose → persistent, distressing low desire in sustained remission: lowering the dose is the common first step; drug holidays are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect
  2. 31-year-old man, one moderate depressive episode in remission 10 months on sertraline dose cut from 150 to 100 mg 2 months ago for low desire still distressed; would rather stop euthymic, full affect, linear thought · no suicidal ideation · HR 70/min → Taper sertraline off gradually → a lower dose failed, and one episode in sustained remission allows stopping; an SSRI is tapered, not stopped abruptly
  3. 27-year-old woman, one depressive episode, in remission 14 months escitalopram lowered 8 weeks ago for low desire desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant No seizures, eating disorder or heart disease euthymic, reactive affect · HR 68/min → Add bupropion to escitalopram → a lower dose failed and she prefers to stay on medication: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine); sildenafil has not been shown to affect desire
  4. 45-year-old man, one depressive episode, in remission 9 months sertraline cut 150 to 100 mg 3 months ago wants to stay on it desire intact; erection trouble since starting it; bothers him euthymic · HR 72/min, BP 126/80 mm Hg → Add sildenafil to sertraline → desire is intact and the problem is arousal, which sildenafil can help; propranolol is unlikely to help, and another SSRI carries a similar risk
  5. 24-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa one depressive episode, in remission on fluoxetine after a dose reduction, desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · HR 66/min · potassium 3.9 mEq/L · euthymic → Switching to bupropion → bupropion has no sexual adverse effects but is contraindicated in bulimia; mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs
  6. 38-year-old woman ran out of paroxetine 4 days ago after 2 years for remitted depression 2 days of nausea, dizziness, unsteady gait, poor sleep brief electric-shock sensations in arms T 37.0 °C · reflexes normal, no clonus · anxious, irritable; mood fine → SSRI discontinuation syndrome → FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping a short half-life drug; relapse comes 2 to 3 weeks or more later, and normal reflexes without clonus argue against serotonin syndrome
  7. 52-year-old man stopped sertraline on his own 3 days ago after 1 year; depression in remission mild nausea, lightheadedness, trouble sleeping wants to stay off T 36.9 °C · reflexes normal, no tremor or clonus · euthymic, mildly irritable · no suicidal ideation → Reassure; it resolves in 1 to 2 weeks → with other serious causes unlikely (afebrile, normal reflexes, no clonus), discontinuation symptoms after an abrupt stop: begin with reassurance that they are reversible and run their course in 1 to 2 weeks; restarting with a slow taper is considered, or support if he prefers not to restart
  8. 35-year-old woman, depression in remission 8 months 2 weeks into a paroxetine taper, 40 mg to 20 mg daily 3 days of dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations irritability keeps her from work T 37.1 °C · no clonus · anxious; mood not depressed → Resume 40 mg and taper more slowly → symptoms during a taper: consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly; fluoxetine is for a slow taper that is poorly tolerated
  9. 42-year-old man, depression in remission 1 year two tries to come off paroxetine, each tapered over 8 weeks both times: dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations relieved by resuming the full dose euthymic · no suicidal ideation · T 36.8 °C → Switch to fluoxetine, then stop → slow tapering is poorly tolerated: consider substituting fluoxetine, whose longer half-life makes discontinuation symptoms less likely
  10. 58-year-old woman taking sertraline got tramadol for back pain this morning 5 hours later: agitated, sweating, nauseated T 38.4 °C · HR 122/min · BP 162/94 mm Hg · dilated pupils · tremor, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus · hyperactive bowel sounds · oriented to person only → Serotonin syndrome → tramadol added to an SSRI, then clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis within hours; neuroleptic malignant syndrome builds over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes
How NBME framed it: question 1

23-year-old woman at a follow-up visit first major depressive episode 1 year ago; fluoxetine 40 mg daily since depression well controlled: enjoys social activities more, more productive at work Reports no suicidal ideation new relationship; concerned about her limited sexual desire vital signs normal · smiling, euthymic affect

Most appropriate next step?

Competing answers
  • Initiate propranolol: an add-on that leaves the antidepressant alone; but it is unlikely to help sexual dysfunction and is not helpful for major depressive disorder.
  • Initiate sildenafil: a treatment for sexual dysfunction; but it helps arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire, her complaint, has been shown.
  • Recommend weekend drug holidays: they seem to spare the relationship; but they are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect.
  • Replace fluoxetine with citalopram: a switch sounds like progress; but citalopram carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction.

Down to two: lowering the dose or switching to citalopram. Lower the dose: her low desire is persistent and distressing, and the explanation says initial management commonly involves decreasing the SSRI dose, especially with sustained remission. If that fails: one episode in sustained remission, so stopping can be considered; or, if she prefers to stay on medication, adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine).

Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: did the mood rise, not fall, after the SSRI started? (antidepressant-induced mania is rare) Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the anxiety new within 3 days of a stop, a hyperarousal symptom of discontinuation?
Transferable rule

Name the effect and its timing before changing the drug. During therapy, with persistent, distressing low desire, lowering the dose is the common first step; typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper, think discontinuation, not relapse.

Thyroid Disease in an Adult

thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) first, then uptake splits making from leaking · levothyroxine recheck timing and its exceptions · the 30% rule and pregnancy-specific normsIs the gland making or leaking, has the TSH had 6 to 8 weeks to settle, and is she pregnant right now?

DiagnosisLevothyroxinePregnancyPractice
Bottom line

Check TSH first, then T4 (thyroxine):

  • Thyrotoxicosis: low TSH with high T4. Radioactive iodine uptake is the next step, but not in a woman who is pregnant (except a molar pregnancy) or breastfeeding.
  • Primary hypothyroidism: high TSH with low T4.
  • Central hypothyroidism: both low, or a normal TSH with a low T4; check cortisol first.
  • High uptake: the gland is making hormone.
  • Low uptake: the hormone is leaking from the gland or is exogenous; antithyroid drugs are useless there.
  • Levothyroxine: TSH lags a dose change by 6 to 8 weeks; pregnancy is the exception, where the dose goes up before the TSH moves.
Diagnosis
Thyroid disease: the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureLabs and uptakeTreatment
Graves diseaseYoung woman; the most common hyperthyroidism; diffuse goiter, with or without a bruit; exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema: Graves onlyTSH-receptor antibodies positive; diffuse high uptakeMethimazole, or propylthiouracil (PTU) in the first trimester; radioactive iodine; or surgery
Toxic multinodular goiter (Plummer)Elderly, longstanding lumpy goiter; apathetic hyperthyroidism: new atrial fibrillation, weight loss, depressionPatchy multifocal hot nodulesRadioactive iodine or surgery; autonomous nodules, not a thyroiditis
Toxic adenomaSingle autonomous noduleOne hot nodule, rest coldRadioactive iodine or lobectomy; hot nodules are almost never cancer
Subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditisPost-viral: painful, tender gland after a viral upper respiratory infection; pain to the jaw or earHigh erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), low uptake; hyper, then hypo, then recoveryNonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), with or without steroids; the only painful thyrotoxicosis
Painless or postpartum thyroiditisPainless small goiter; classically 2 to 6 months postpartumThyroid peroxidase (TPO) antibodies positive, low uptake, normal ESRBeta-blocker only: nothing is being made
Hashimoto thyroiditisThe most common hypothyroidism; firm, rubbery goiter; may have a brief hashitoxicosisAnti-TPO; Hürthle cells, germinal centersLevothyroxine; a rapidly enlarging gland points to B-cell lymphoma
Factitious thyrotoxicosisSupplements or healthcare access; no goiterLow uptake and low thyroglobulinStop the hormone; thyroglobulin is high when a gland leaks
Riedel thyroiditis, IgG4 (immunoglobulin G subclass 4)-relatedRock-hard, fixed, painless; mimics anaplastic carcinomaFibrosis, IgG4 plasma cellsSteroids or tamoxifen; young and hard: Riedel; old: anaplastic
Thyroid storm (emergency)Fever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium; precipitant: surgery, infection, iodine loadClinical diagnosis: do not wait for labsBeta-blocker, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids (iodine first fuels synthesis)
Central hypothyroidismHypothyroid with other pituitary deficits; after Sheehan syndrome, a mass or apoplexyTSH low or normal with a low T4Titrate to free T4, not TSH; screen cortisol first
Levothyroxine titration
Recheck timing and its exceptions Recheck interval – TSH lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks; earlier values are untrustworthy. At 8 weeks it is reliable: a TSH of 9.5 then means the dose is genuinely inadequate, so increase it · Rechecked too soon – under 6 weeks after a change: recheck in 6 weeks, not a dose change (outside pregnancy; in pregnancy, TSH may be rechecked 4 to 6 weeks after a change) · TSH stays high despite escalating doses – adherence, then absorption: empty stomach; iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors and cholestyramine bind it; consider celiac disease · Elderly or coronary artery disease – start low, go slow (25 to 50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia · Central hypothyroidism – titrate to free T4; TSH is the broken variable · Subclinical hypothyroidism – high TSH, normal T4: treat if TSH is over 10, TPO-positive, pregnant, or symptomatic · Pregnancy – levothyroxine requirements frequently increase, usually by 25 to 50%; increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
Hypothyroidism in pregnancy

Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG). β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) shares an alpha subunit with TSH and stimulates the TSH receptor. As a result, a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own; a patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate.

The 30% rule Dose rule – increase levothyroxine by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with a currently normal TSH; do not wait for the TSH to rise · Monitoring – TSH may be checked at confirmation, approximately every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy, at least once in the third trimester, and 4 to 6 weeks after any dose change, using pregnancy-specific norms; target a TSH between the lower limit of the reference range and 2.5 mU/L. Free T4 (analog assay) is an appropriate marker in the first half of pregnancy · Mechanism – estrogen raises TBG, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need. Separately, β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which lowers TSH in the first trimester · Drug – levothyroxine; T3 (triiodothyronine), given as liothyronine, is never the right drug in pregnancy · Graves disease in pregnancy – PTU is the recommended drug in the first trimester (American Thyroid Association, 2017); whether to switch to methimazole after it is a clinical choice; never radioactive iodine
Thyroid labs in normal first-trimester pregnancy
HormoneChangeInterpretation
Total T4IncreasedPhysiologic: TBG excess binds more hormone
Free T4Unchanged or mildly increasedThe value to trust in the first half of pregnancy
TSHDecreasedβ-hCG cross-reactivity: not hyperthyroidism
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman has 6 weeks of heat intolerance and tremor small, nontender goiter no eye signs; no pretibial skin change Not breastfeeding; no neck pain or recent illness HR 104/min · TSH low · free T4 high · urine pregnancy test negative → Radioactive iodine uptake → thyrotoxicosis with no sign that names the cause, in a woman who is neither pregnant nor breastfeeding: radioactive iodine uptake splits a gland making hormone (high uptake) from one leaking it or exogenous hormone (low uptake). Thyroid ultrasound shows structure, not function, and cannot split making from leaking; fine-needle aspiration is for a cold nodule
  2. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism returns for a dose check Started levothyroxine 8 weeks ago; takes it daily on an empty stomach still tired; no palpitations HR 62/min · BP 118/76 mm Hg · TSH 9.5 mU/L → Increase the dose → TSH lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks; at 8 weeks it is reliable, so a TSH of 9.5 means the dose is genuinely inadequate: increase it. Rechecking in 6 weeks is the answer only for a value drawn too soon
  3. 32-year-old woman has 3 months of weight loss and palpitations diffuse goiter with a bruit proptosis of both eyes No neck pain HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Graves disease → a diffuse goiter with a bruit and proptosis: proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves disease only, so they make the diagnosis, and uptake is diffusely high. Toxic multinodular goiter is a lumpy gland in an older patient with patchy uptake; subacute thyroiditis is painful, with low uptake
  4. 28-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has a positive home pregnancy test On a stable levothyroxine dose for 3 years feels well; no palpitations or fatigue HR 74/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 1.8 mU/L → Increase the dose by about 30% now → a patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate, so increase levothyroxine by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week) as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, even with a currently normal TSH, then TSH may be rechecked in about 4 weeks. Waiting until the TSH rises is the titration rule in the wrong slot; liothyronine is never the right drug in pregnancy
  5. 40-year-old woman has 1 week of neck pain radiating to the jaw Sore throat 3 weeks ago thyroid painful and very tender uptake scan: low uptake T 37.9 °C · HR 106/min · TSH low · ESR 88 mm/h → Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis → a painful, tender gland after a viral upper respiratory infection, with pain to the jaw, a high ESR and low uptake: the only painful thyrotoxicosis. It runs hyper, then hypo, then recovery; treat with NSAIDs, with or without steroids. Hashimoto thyroiditis is a firm, rubbery goiter with anti-TPO antibodies; painless thyroiditis has a normal ESR
  6. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has her TSH rechecked Her levothyroxine dose was increased 3 weeks ago takes each dose on an empty stomach feels better; not pregnant HR 66/min · BP 120/78 mm Hg · TSH 8 mU/L → Make no change → make no change and recheck in 6 weeks: outside pregnancy, a TSH rechecked under 6 weeks after a change is untrustworthy, because it lags dose changes by 6 to 8 weeks. A dose change now reacts to a value that has not settled
  7. 55-year-old woman with untreated hyperthyroidism is brought in for agitation Received iodinated contrast for imaging 3 days ago confused and diaphoretic no neck stiffness; lungs clear T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 156/min · BP 150/60 mm Hg → Thyroid storm → fever, tachyarrhythmia and delirium in a thyrotoxic patient after an iodine load: a clinical diagnosis, so treatment does not wait for labs. Give a beta-blocker, then a thionamide (PTU), then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids. Graves disease without storm lacks the fever and delirium. Sepsis has no evident source (lungs clear, no neck stiffness), while untreated hyperthyroidism after an iodine load, a known storm precipitant, explains the whole picture
  8. 30-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is seen at 9 weeks' gestation Asymptomatic apart from mild morning nausea no goiter; no eye signs HR 84/min · TSH 0.3 mU/L · total T4 elevated · free T4 high-normal → Normal pregnancy physiology → in a normal first trimester, total T4 rises because excess thyroxine-binding globulin binds more hormone, and TSH falls from β-hCG cross-reactivity: physiology, not hyperthyroidism, so no treatment. Free T4 is the value to trust, and it distinguishes physiology from Graves disease
  9. 45-year-old woman has 6 months of fatigue, weight gain and constipation firm, rubbery, nontender goiter Feels cold when others are comfortable positive TPO antibodies HR 58/min · TSH high · free T4 low → Hashimoto thyroiditis → a firm, rubbery goiter with anti-TPO antibodies and primary hypothyroidism is the most common hypothyroidism; treat with levothyroxine. Hürthle cells and germinal centers are its histology. Subacute thyroiditis is painful; Riedel thyroiditis is rock-hard, fixed and painless
  10. 44-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has a persistently high TSH Takes levothyroxine each morning together with her calcium supplement reports taking every dose; no other medications HR 60/min · BP 118/74 mm Hg · TSH 7.8 mU/L → Separate them by 4 hours → a TSH that stays high despite the dose: adherence first, then absorption. Iron, calcium, proton pump inhibitors and cholestyramine bind levothyroxine, so it is taken on an empty stomach: separate the calcium from it by 4 hours rather than raising the dose. Consider celiac disease when absorption is the problem
  11. 30-year-old woman has 3 weeks of palpitations and anxiety Delivered 3 months ago; not breastfeeding small, painless, nontender goiter; no eye signs uptake scan: low uptake HR 108/min · BP 124/76 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Postpartum thyroiditis → painless thyrotoxicosis 2 to 6 months postpartum with low uptake; TPO antibodies are typically positive and the ESR normal. Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is painful and tender; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule with the rest cold
  12. 28-year-old woman at 8 weeks' gestation was diagnosed with Graves disease today diffuse goiter with a bruit; mild proptosis First pregnancy; no prior thyroid treatment HR 112/min · BP 128/72 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Propylthiouracil → PTU is the recommended drug in the first trimester (American Thyroid Association, 2017), not methimazole, because PTU generally carries a lower risk of birth defects than methimazole; whether to switch to methimazole after it is a clinical choice. Radioactive iodine is never an option in pregnancy
  13. 44-year-old woman on levothyroxine has 3 weeks of palpitations Dose increased 10 weeks ago fine tremor; warm, moist skin No new medications or supplements HR 108/min · BP 132/70 mm Hg · TSH 0.05 mU/L → Decrease the dose → a TSH of 0.05 with palpitations, drawn after the 6 to 8 week lag, is a reliable value: the dose is too high, so decrease it. Continuing the same dose leaves it too high
  14. 28-year-old woman, a nurse, has 2 months of palpitations and weight loss no goiter; thyroid nontender No recent pregnancy or neck pain uptake scan: low uptake HR 110/min · TSH low · free T4 high · thyroglobulin low → Factitious thyrotoxicosis → low uptake with a low thyroglobulin and no goiter is exogenous hormone (supplements or healthcare access): stop the hormone. Thyroglobulin is high when an inflamed gland leaks, as in painless thyroiditis; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule
  15. 31-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 6 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was increased today She asks when her thyroid tests will be repeated mild nausea; no palpitations HR 76/min · BP 110/68 mm Hg → TSH in 4 weeks → TSH may be checked approximately every 4 weeks during the first half of pregnancy and 4 to 6 weeks after any dose change, using pregnancy-specific norms, with a target between the lower limit of the reference range and 2.5 mU/L. The next-trimester visit is too late for a dose changed today, and weekly testing is far more often than the roughly 4-week schedule
  16. 55-year-old woman is delirious the day after a hip fracture repair Graves disease diagnosed 3 years ago agitated, diaphoretic, tremulous T 40.0 °C · atrial fibrillation, HR 160/min · BP 146/58 mm Hg → Beta-blocker → thyroid storm after surgery: the beta-blocker comes first, then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids. Potassium iodide given first fuels hormone synthesis
  17. 78-year-old woman has new primary hypothyroidism Coronary artery disease with stable angina; stent 2 years ago fatigue, dry skin, constipation HR 56/min · BP 134/80 mm Hg · TSH 14 mU/L · free T4 low → Start low and titrate slowly → elderly or with coronary artery disease: start low and go slow (25 to 50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia
  18. 68-year-old woman has 2 months of weight loss and low mood Neck swelling for many years irregular, multinodular gland; no eye signs uptake scan: patchy, several hot areas HR 104/min, irregularly irregular · TSH low → Toxic multinodular goiter → an elderly patient with a longstanding, lumpy goiter and patchy multifocal hot nodules: autonomous nodules, not a thyroiditis, often with apathetic hyperthyroidism (new atrial fibrillation, weight loss, depression). Treat with radioactive iodine or surgery. Graves disease takes up diffusely; a toxic adenoma is one hot nodule with the rest cold
  19. 27-year-old woman with hypothyroidism plans to conceive in 6 months Takes liothyronine twice daily palpitations some afternoons; tired by evening No other medications HR 82/min · BP 114/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.4 mU/L → Switch to levothyroxine before conception → T3 has a short half-life with wide level swings, and liothyronine is never the right drug in pregnancy: switch to levothyroxine before conception. Adding levothyroxine keeps the liothyronine
  20. 30-year-old woman has palpitations 3 months after delivery small, painless goiter positive TPO antibodies low radioactive iodine uptake Not breastfeeding; no neck pain or fever HR 112/min · BP 122/74 mm Hg · TSH low · free T4 high → Beta-blocker alone → low uptake means nothing is being made, so antithyroid drugs such as methimazole are useless: a beta-blocker only, for the symptoms
  21. 44-year-old woman on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism has a positive home pregnancy test Dose stable for 2 years; TSH normal 6 months ago feels well; mild breast tenderness HR 72/min · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Increase the dose by about 30% and recheck → levothyroxine requirements frequently increase in pregnancy, usually by 25 to 50%: increase the dose as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, by 20 to 30% (for example, two extra daily doses a week), and TSH may be rechecked in about 4 weeks, without waiting for the TSH to rise. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment
  22. 29-year-old woman with hypothyroidism is 10 weeks pregnant Her levothyroxine dose was raised when pregnancy was confirmed total T4 elevated; free T4 normal HR 78/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · TSH 2.0 mU/L → Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulin → estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, so more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; as pregnancy progresses, transfer of maternal T4 to the fetus and T4 degradation by placental type 3 deiodinase add to the need; the added degradation is placental, not hepatic. At 10 weeks, thyroxine-binding globulin is still rising toward its peak near week 16. β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor, which is why TSH falls in the first trimester; it also stimulates thyroid hormone production, so it does not explain the rising requirement.
Paired pearls Lid lag and stare occur in any thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic); proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves only. A hot nodule is almost never cancer; a cold nodule needs fine-needle aspiration. Nodule workup starts with TSH: if low, get an uptake scan; if normal or high, get an ultrasound, then fine-needle aspiration.
Pregnancy pearls Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment, because the fetus depends on maternal T4 early. A low TSH with a high total T4 in the first trimester is physiology, not Graves; free T4 distinguishes the two.
Common wrong answers Antithyroid workup for a TSH of 0.3 in early pregnancy: β-hCG cross-reactivity explains the low TSH. “Recheck in 6 to 8 weeks” at conception: correct as a titration rule, but pregnancy is the one setting where acting first is right.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the neonatal version, where the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect.
Transferable rule

Apply an exception to the standard titration rule only when its trigger condition is actually present; otherwise, follow the standard rule. When physiology predictably outruns a fixed drug dose, adjust the dose pre-emptively; do not recheck and react, although that approach is correct in every other setting.
